## Run resumption

Resume an interrupted Harbor run only when its model, checked-out repository revision, runtime
limit, and dataset state are unchanged. Read the original run ID and effective configuration from
its durable `record.json`. Use the model and Harbor config from the same Marin commit, then add the
original run ID:

```bash
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model-config "$CAMPAIGN/model-configs/<model-config>.yaml" \
  --harbor-config "$STAGED_HARBOR_DIR/<harbor-config>.yaml" \
  --resume-run-id <original-run-id>
```

The durable `<records-prefix>/<original-run-id>/results/harbor_jobs/` tree must remain accessible.
Harbor preserves completed scored trials and reruns missing attempts and exceptions in its pinned
resume taxonomy. Use a clean replacement when model, policy, pins, limits, records prefix, or
dataset state changed, or when the unscored error is outside that taxonomy. Never delete a trial
directory to force recovery.

## Baseline-specific launch settings

The YAML files under
`experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/model-configs/` are authoritative for checkpoint and tokenizer
revisions, serving context, GPU count, tensor and data parallelism, reasoning parser, tool parser,
sampling overrides, and Pi `thinking_format`. Use the matching file unchanged. Pi uses
`qwen-chat-template` for Qwen3.6 and Qwen3-Next and `chat-template` for the other models.

## Updating codebase pins

Use the newest campaign pin for each codebase across the full release, assuming forward
compatibility with earlier score-producing runs. If a pin change causes an observed result
regression, stop launches, fix or revert the change, and issue a new policy version when the
evaluation behavior intentionally changes. Preserve the original run's exact pins in its immutable
config snapshot even after the release-wide pins advance.

## Standards for presenting Marin evals

* Display score cells in the standard tracker and any tournament-only tracker to three significant digits. Apply the same convention to a tracker formed from their union. The linked durable run records retain unrounded scores. Tournament and figure analyses recover full-precision task aggregates from that durable evidence; tracker values are presentation-only.
* Select the release Snowball checkpoint by the uncertainty-aware paired tournament defined in “How do we choose which model to release?” Release figures include only the selected checkpoint, not the other Snowball candidates. The Snowball candidate family includes Grug 67B A2B checkpoints as well as checkpoints named Snowball. For each benchmark, plot the selected Snowball checkpoint and every non-Snowball baseline with an available score and total-training-FLOP estimate. Performance is on the y-axis and total training FLOPs are on a logarithmic x-axis. A baseline with an incomplete suite may appear in the scatterplots for its completed benchmarks, but it is excluded from cross-benchmark critical-difference analysis unless it has the full common benchmark panel.
* Produce uncertainty-aware normalized critical-difference diagrams with and without a FLOP control. Normalize scores within each benchmark across the complete-panel cohort. Estimate each score's task-level sample SEM from the scored trial rewards, then multiply the SEM by `1 / sqrt(0.9)` to account conservatively for the policy's 10% infrastructure-failure tolerance. With a fixed random seed, draw 100,000 score panels from independent normal sampling distributions centered on the reported scores and clipped to the metric's `[0, 1]` range. Rank models within every benchmark for each draw, using average ranks for ties, and report mean ranks with simultaneous 95% bands based on the draw-wise maximum absolute rank deviation. Report the Nemenyi critical difference at `alpha = 0.05`; it depends on the number of models and benchmarks, while score uncertainty affects the simulated rank distribution and its simultaneous bands.
* For the FLOP-controlled diagram, regress the draw's benchmark-normalized scores on `log10(total training FLOPs)` with one common linear slope, rank the within-benchmark residuals, and otherwise use the same uncertainty procedure. Treat FLOP estimates as fixed point estimates and disclose that their estimation uncertainty is not propagated. The uncontrolled diagram ranks the sampled normalized scores directly.
* We use a 6ND proxy for pretraining FLOPS, and 6 * max_tokens_per_rollout / max_context_length * n_rollouts * active_params proxy for RL FLOPS; that said, we are the only lab, as of this writing, which releases RL FLOPS, so meaningful comparisons are impossible. From the few labs who release midtraining / SFT information, we derive an unweighted mean percentage of FLOPS devoted to midtraining. We then estimate midtraining FLOPS for other labs using that mean. We estimate total FLOPS as the sum of pretraining FLOPS + (all midtraining / non-RL) FLOPS + (all RL and OPD) FLOPS. For any model which doesn't give sufficient evidence for any of the three stages, use the mean FLOPS over all models in the cohort as the estimated  FLOPS for that stage.
* In a separate standalone table, include all raw scores in XX.y format, with 95% confidence intervals derived from the trial count and the infrastructure error tolerance -- do not leave gaps, use table captions for results that require further context, use the exact same model family in the table as was present in the x-y scatterplot(s)
* Eval results are reportable IFF the eval in question completed with no more than 10% of trials encountering infrastructure errors
* Eval results are reportable IFF they include provenance, in the form of model traces, and where available, verifier traces
* Any eval result that is publicly presented should clearly distinguish whether the benchmarks are in-distribution (part of the dev set), held out, or a mix of the two
* Any eval result that is publicly presented in a major release should report on *all* ID and OOD benchmarks, avoiding cherry picking, substitution, or new evals outside of a formal policy update
* For active development and internal communication, it is fine to define working subsets of the ID benchmarks and report on those in isolation

### Reproduce SOTOPIA-hard length control

SOTOPIA-Hard length control was introduced post-hoc, after the agent traces were generated. For this generation of eval policy, it needs to be run separately. The details on how to do so live here.

The Harbor verifier writes the unadjusted normalized overall reward and
`sotopia_response_characters` for every completed episode. The release score is a cohort
statistic, so it must be regenerated across all compared models rather than copied from one
Harbor run's aggregate. From the pinned Marin checkout, with CoreWeave S3 read credentials and
the campaign tracker available locally, run:

```bash
TRACKER=/absolute/path/to/TRACKER.md
OUTPUT_DIR=/absolute/path/to/artifacts/sotopia-length-controlled-overall
uv run python experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/analysis/sotopia_length_control/rank.py \
  --tracker "$TRACKER" --output-dir "$OUTPUT_DIR"
```

The tool reads the seven dimension scores and transcripts from each sealed SOTOPIA-hard archive,
measures only the evaluated agent's emitted characters, and groups cross-validation folds by task.
It writes both raw and length-controlled rankings, plus the tracker SHA-256, every source archive,
the selected regularization strength, and all cross-validation losses. Its counterfactual sets the
response-length difference to zero relative to each task's cohort median. Adding or removing a
model changes that median and requires recomputing the complete cohort. A policy-valid
infrastructure failure retains its configured zero; unscored infrastructure failures are excluded
under the campaign's sealing rule.

The tracker-linked October 15 cohort output is preserved at
`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/ablations/sotopia-overall-length-controlled-20261015-c5ef5789/`.

### Reproduce the Snowball tournament and critical-difference figures

Use the campaign tracker as a point-in-time input: every numeric cell must contain its durable
S3 result link, either a native `/results` archive or a corrected per-trial replay JSON. The
tournament requires complete observed scores for every Snowball or Grug candidate on its
23-benchmark selection panel; it excludes FinanceBench, PIQA, and TriviaQA. It derives each cell's
full-precision task aggregate and task-level SEM from the durable trial evidence, then expands the
SEM by `1 / sqrt(0.9)`. The three-decimal tracker score is presentation-only. A benchmark is a
win only when `abs(score_a - score_b) > 1.96 * hypot(adjusted_sem_a, adjusted_sem_b)`; otherwise it
is a tie. A win is one vote, a tie half a vote, and each candidate's selection statistic is the
unweighted mean of its paired win rates against the other candidates. Preserve the generated
tracker and recovered-metrics SHA-256 values, and do not combine a tournament selection with
figures generated from a different tracker snapshot.

The analysis tools are in the Marin campaign worktree under
`experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/analysis/`, in the
`snowball_tournament/` and `critical_difference/` subdirectories. From the pinned Marin checkout,
with the campaign tracker and output directory available locally, run:

```bash
TRACKER=/absolute/path/to/TRACKER.md
OUTPUT_DIR=/absolute/path/to/artifacts
uv run python experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/analysis/snowball_tournament/pairwise.py \
  --tracker "$TRACKER" --recovered-metrics "$OUTPUT_DIR/recovered-record-metrics.json" \
  --output-dir "$OUTPUT_DIR/snowball-tournament"
uv run python experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/analysis/critical_difference/plot.py \
  --tracker "$TRACKER" --selection "$OUTPUT_DIR/snowball-tournament/snowball_selection.json" \
  --recovered-metrics "$OUTPUT_DIR/recovered-record-metrics.json" \
  --output-dir "$OUTPUT_DIR/critical-difference"
```

Both commands need read access to the scored results in CoreWeave S3; configure the normal
Marin `fsutil` credentials first. It reads canonical `record.json` files for trial counts and
normalized sample rewards for non-binary metrics. If a NUPA record has not been written, the
tool requires its sealed native Evalchemy archive and verifies its coverage and canonical score.
For cells sealed from an interrupted executor,
`recovered-record-metrics.json` supplies the independently aggregated scored-trial count and
reward standard error; retain that audit file with the tracker. The complete-panel cohort is the selected
Snowball plus the non-Snowball models listed in `critical_difference/baseline_flops.csv`; a
benchmark enters the diagrams only if every cohort model has a numeric, linked score. The output
includes every benchmark-level pair outcome, the full paired-win matrix and selection summary,
per-cell sample statistics, FLOP estimates, rank tables, and uncontrolled and FLOP-controlled PNG,
PDF, and SVG figures. Regenerate
both commands after any tracker change. The uncertainty, normalization, FLOP-control, and
critical-difference calculations are defined above; the random seed and draw count are fixed in
the plotting code.

## Future considerations

* We would like to post-train multiple Snowball checkpoints, experimenting with different degrees of compute applied to post-training, to establish trade-off lines / domains
* We would like to think about a "marin model card" that would set minimum standards for true open development
* amd/Instella-MoE-16B-A3B-Think is not runnable currently from our pinned vLLM fork, but we would like to look at this model in the future
* We still weren't able to land a trusted K2 Horizon baseline set of scores yet
* evaluate our baselines on OOD as well as ID
* JudgeArena multilingual, maybe one of those cultural idiom / include benchmarks, restore simpleQA-mini, a long context supplement for MRCR
* Produce a summary of why we think the previously flagged TB2 / TB4 task description overlap are likely not problematic, if they are not
* Find a better instruction following benchmark than IFBench
* Consider a smaller subset of MMLU-Pro and NUPA so they run faster
* Fix the inconsistency in Evalchemy timeout error handling
* In the future, we may deliberately use subsets of very large benchmarks like BFCL and NUPA as training material; in this case, we must mark the full benchmarks as explicitly contaminated, adding a new section to our eval policy
* Properly unify on the co-hosted MiniMax judge
* Consider using a judge panel and requiring all judges to agree on equivalence
* Consider using cruxeval input as well as output
* Drop PIQA as non-discriminating, TriviaQA needs its grader reconsidered
* biomedical knowledge: MedXpertQA or PubMedQA, Clinical reasoning: HealthBench Professional/ Bedside Bench /ASCENT, Biological discovery: Longevity — genetics regression; LAB-Bench cloning / DNA methylation age comparison, Medical coding: MedConceptsQA — ATC Hard/ MedConceptsQA ICD-10 procedures, hard

topics.title: Acquire pinned Harbor Hub releases through the curation cache
topics.body:
Acquire pinned Harbor Hub releases through the existing cached source-download stage. A declaration supplies the Hub release digest; the exporter checks that Harbor resolves that release, verifies each task's native content digest, and records the resolved task list alongside the package rows for conversion.

Acquisition downloads the full release, one package at a time, with curation sampling afterward, matching the HF source path. Existing local-input overrides bypass downloading for bounded development runs. Cache identity includes the release, exporter, and pinned Harbor commit, so unrelated runtime dependency updates do not invalidate acquisition. Interrupted exports reuse completed task rows; partial writes do not count as complete. Dataset-level scoring files remain unsupported; linked or oversized packages produce unsupported rows; the 8 MiB export ceiling is distinct from a recipe’s resource budget.

Harbor resolves release membership. A separate SDK manifest checksum is not required: it differs from the Hub release identifier for the inspected Skill2Env release, and the cause of that mismatch is unconfirmed. Per-task content verification remains independent of release resolution.

Six focused acquisition/export cases and mechanical lint passed locally, including interrupted-download recovery and cache reuse after unrelated runtime dependency changes. The unified-unit workflow now runs exporter tests in the frozen Harbor project when selected; CI must validate the updated head. A bounded export verified one real Skill2Env task. Full-release acquisition and remote-storage export remain untested.

Skill2Env conversion is a dependent change in #10154. Part of #9630.

🤖 Holistic review of a7ba420c0843c4243b27398b612ce98735b296b4.

Adds `HarborHubSource` and runs a Harbor-runtime exporter as a subprocess inside the existing cached download step. Each task is checked against its pinned content digest and written as task-reference-keyed JSONL. The design fits the source/download split and I found no blockers. The main gaps: CI never runs the exporter test, and the cache key changes with every Harbor lock bump.

**Should fix**
1. `experiments/post_training/task_curation/tests/test_harbor_hub.py:10` `importorskip("harbor")` skips this test in every CI leg, because `harbor` is not in the workspace environment. It is the only test that covers `export_release`: the release-digest check, the per-task hash check, duplicate references, and the `metadata.files` rejection. I ran it under `uv run --isolated --project config/external/harbor --frozen --with pytest` and it passes. To get it into CI, call it through the runtime the way `tests/evaluation/test_harbor_trial_driver.py` reaches `config/external/harbor`, or add a CI step that runs this file in that project.
2. `experiments/post_training/task_curation/pipeline.py:603` `runtime_sha256` hashes the whole `config/external/harbor/uv.lock`. The dependency updater (`scripts/ci/dependency_update_policy.py:32`) rewrites that lock on its regular schedule, including for unrelated pins such as daytona and litellm. Each rewrite re-keys the download artifact and every downstream curation identity, which triggers a full re-download, even though the per-task digest check already pins the bytes. Key on the locked `harbor` git commit instead. `harbor_runtime_descriptor` in `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/driver_config.py:80` already parses it out of the lock.
3. `experiments/post_training/task_curation/pipeline.py:100` and `:680` rebuild the isolated-runtime path and the `uv run --isolated --project … --frozen python` command. `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/driver_config.py` already owns these as `HARBOR_RUNTIME_PROJECT`, `_harbor_env_dir` (uses `find_project_root`) and `_driver_command`. `parents[3]` breaks silently if this module moves. Resolve the project through `HARBOR_RUNTIME_PROJECT` plus `find_project_root`, and share the command builder.
4. `experiments/post_training/task_curation/harbor_hub.py:67` The body says acquisition matches the HF source path. The HF path resumes (`write_jsonl(..., skip_existing=True)` at `pipeline.py:671`); this loop does not, so a failed step re-downloads the whole release one task at a time. Skip refs whose `tasks/<sha256(ref)>.jsonl` already exists. The filename is already a function of the immutable reference, so a resumed run writes the same bytes. Then drop "Use a fresh output directory per export" from `docs/references/task-curation.md`.
5. `experiments/post_training/task_curation/harbor_hub.py:23` `MAX_TASK_BYTES = 8 MiB` writes `unsupported: resources_over_budget` into the shared download artifact. That is the same reason code the pipeline uses for the per-recipe `CurationRecipe.resource_budget_bytes` (default 1 MB). A recipe that raises its budget above 8 MiB still gets those tasks deferred, and the catalog cannot tell the exporter's ceiling from the recipe's own. Emit a distinct reason such as `export_size_ceiling`, and document the ceiling next to `resource_budget_bytes`.

**Related PRs**
6. #10154 (Skill2Env conversion) is based on this branch and consumes the `unsupported` rows from `export_task`. Merge this PR first.
7. #10181 adds `type RecipeSource = HfSource | UrlSource | ArtifactSource` across the same `pipeline.py` annotations that this PR widens inline (9 occurrences). Adopt one alias here so the repeated unions go away. Whichever PR lands second adds its class to `RecipeSource`; merge order between them doesn't matter.

topics.title: [rolloutengine] Replace task sessions with registered harnesses
topics.body:
RolloutEngine runs each task attempt through a harness, which owns the agent loop and calls the model only through a `RolloutRecorder`. `RolloutEngine(machine_factories, harnesses, *, observer=None)` holds the two registries, and `run_task(spec, model, *, run_id=None)` returns a `GradedRollout(rollout, grade)`. `Rollout` replaces `RolloutData`: it holds `run_id`, one `ConversationRecord` for each conversation of the attempt, the stop reason, metrics, and run outputs, and no longer carries `task_id` or the grade. Without a `run_id`, each attempt gets a new random ID, so the events of repeated attempts of a task stay apart.

A harness implements `Harness`: `check(task, limits)` rejects a task before any machine starts, and `run(context, recorder)` runs one attempt with a `HarnessContext(task, machine, events, cleanup, run_id)`. This replaces `TaskSession`, `TaskSessionFactory`, and `TaskGrader`. The recorder's `start(prompt)` begins a conversation, `reply(observations, token_ids=...)` continues it, and `record(observations=..., data=..., metrics=...)` adds to the step of the last turn. The recorder records the exact tokens and applies `max_turns`, `max_total_tokens`, the length stop, `model_turn_timeout`, and `tool_turn_timeout`. The next request after a limit raises `LimitReached`, and a failed model request raises `RolloutEnded` with the model's error as its cause. A second `start` is a new conversation, so `Transition.reset` and the engine's reset rules are removed, and the rollout keeps every conversation. Harnesses do not grade. `SessionGrader` and harness grading are removed, the engine grades the last conversation that has a model turn with the task's grader, and a harness puts its own rewards in step data. Thus a new conversation whose first request fails leaves the earlier one to grade. `harness_rollout(harness, task, model, *, limits, machine=None, ...)` runs a harness without the engine, and `task_machine(task, factory, runtime, *, cleanup_timeout)` starts a task machine for it.

`shell_harness(command_timeout=..., shell_tool=..., tools=...)` takes the shell options and tool providers that were in the spec and the engine, so one engine can register several shell configurations. `step_harness(open_episode)` runs a step-style `Episode` (`prepare`, `advance`, `close`). `agent_harness(run)` replaces `AgentTaskSession`. Each `complete` call of the agent runs the recorder in the caller's task, with no queue and no request tasks. One model request can be open at a time. A call that is cancelled while the model generates loses that generation and does not change the record, and the last prompt again gets the same turn. After the attempt ends, calls wait until the cleanup, after grading, so a waiting agent does not change the task machine during grading. The cleanup then cancels the agent, and an agent that does not stop within `cleanup_timeout` is a cleanup error.

When the harness ends or a turn deadline expires, the record is final. The recorder cancels a model call that is still open, for example in an agent's HTTP handler, and ignores its result, so the grader and the returned rollout see the same record. A harness registers the close of its resources with `context.cleanup`. The closes run after grading, each within `cleanup_timeout`, and a failure is a cleanup error of the attempt.

`TaskRolloutSpec(task, harness, task_machine, verifier_machine, limits, trace, judge_connection)` replaces `LoweredTaskSpec`, `TaskRuntimeSpec`, and `TaskSessionSpec`. `RolloutEngine.check(spec)`, which `run_task` also calls first, replaces `lower_task` and `validate_lowered_task`. `Prompt` replaces `SessionStart`. `ModelRequest.continuation`, a `Continuation(served_token_ids, assistant_message_index)`, replaces `prefix_token_ids` and `assistant_message_index`. A request has a continuation, pinned `prompt_token_ids`, or neither, and a `MESSAGES` rollout never has a continuation. In `Transition`, `token_ids` replaces `next_prompt_token_ids`, and `next_options` is removed, so options change only with a new conversation. `reward`, `token_rewards`, `token_credit`, `reward_components`, and the per-step `grade` are removed from `Transition`. A harness can put such values in its new `data` field, which the engine keeps unchanged. A trainer that reads per-token rewards from it compares their length with the turn's `response_token_ids`; `RolloutStep.response_end` is the index of the turn's last response token. `check` also rejects, for every harness, a shell binding without a task machine, as it already did for the shell capability, and a graded `state` task, because the engine does not capture state.

A judge grader grades on the host through `grade_remote_judge_answer`, the function that the curation pipelines use, with `judge_connection` or with `VERIFYIT_JUDGE_BASE_URL` and `VERIFYIT_JUDGE_API_KEY`. It uses no verifier machine. `judge_connection` holds an API key, so it is never serialized. `check` rejects a judge task with a verifier machine, a judge task with no connection and no `VERIFYIT_JUDGE_BASE_URL`, and a judge task whose answer is not in the conversation. The verifier deadline stops the engine's wait for a host judge, but the judge call ends only at its own `JudgeSpec.request_timeout`.

An interrupted attempt raises `RolloutInterrupted(rollout, operation)` from `harness_rollout`, and `GradedRolloutInterrupted`, with the grade of the completed turns, from `run_task`. A model failure still grades the completed turns. `RolloutContractError` means only a token-contract violation.

The token trace grows its loss mask and log probabilities as lists, and the rollout is built once at the end. With a fake model that costs nothing, engine time per turn falls from 2.4–2.5 to 1.0–1.1 ms at 129k tokens and from 4.7–5.0 to 2.6 ms at 257k tokens (three runs each against 24aa43cea).

MarinSkyRL pins rolloutengine at a Marin commit, so it keeps working until it advances that pin. Its port must:

- run its step-style sessions through `step_harness`, and put each old `grade()` result in the last step's data
- give Nemotron its own harness, which calls `start` again for its correction turn
- read `rollout.conversations` when it builds training samples
- register one shell harness for each shell configuration
- build its `ChatContinuation` from `ModelRequest.continuation`
- read `result.rollout` and `result.grade` from `run_task`, and `grade` from `GradedRolloutInterrupted`
- take task IDs from its specs, and rebuild its stored task Parquet files, which hold `LoweredTaskSpec` JSON
- drop `RolloutOperation.CLEANUP`, which the engine never raised

Observers get `run_id` instead of `run_key`, `ConversationStarted` for each conversation instead of `SessionPrepared`, `TransitionCompleted` without `reset_conversation`, and the cleanup steps `episode_close`, `agent_stop`, and `tool_provider_close` instead of `session_close`.

Part of #10187.

comments.body:
🤖 One question on grading while this is a draft, from the Taskforge side; nothing here needs to block the PR.

`Harness.grade` now grades only a `SessionGrader` task, and `_grade_rollout` grades every other task with the task's grader: in process when a verifyit grader has no environment, otherwise in the verifier machine. A verifyit `JudgeSpec` grader must carry an environment, because the judge mode has no in-process grader (`Mode.JUDGE` has no candidate entry in `verifyit/spec.py`, so `candidate_spec` refuses it), so every judge task goes to a verifier machine, and `check_spec` requires one. TaskCompendium's own entry grades the same task differently: `runtime/task_grading.py` `grade_task` sends any `JudgeSpec` grader to `grade_remote_judge_answer(task, attempt, judge_connection)` on the host before it looks at the environment, and the task-curation verification and controls pipelines use that path.

Would a host-graded judge fit this shape as a third registry? Something like `RolloutEngine(machine_factories, harnesses, judges)`, with `RolloutSpec.judge: str | None` naming the registered judge (a callable from task and `GradingAttempt` to `GradeResult`, the default built from `grade_remote_judge_answer` and a `JudgeConnection`), `check_spec` accepting `verifier_machine=None` for a `JudgeSpec` grader when a judge is selected, and `_grade_rollout` running it under `asyncio.to_thread` like `grade_answer`. The task definition stays unchanged and nothing in it names a service, which keeps #10021's line. If you would rather take it as a follow-up PR after this one lands, I can draft it against this branch's shape; a word on which you prefer is all I need.

Context: Taskforge's decision-model verifier (judge graded on the host through a service the lowering selects) cannot be validated through the engine until a judge grades host-side, and today no engine test exercises a `JudgeSpec` grader.

🤖 Holistic review of 8e0ca5234a0f783fa3d39a26409c09d8052cc6cf.

> **In short:** The diff replaces the 3–9 day old `TaskSession`/`LoweredTaskSpec` API with named `Harness` records and a flat `RolloutSpec`. It also adds `ManagedAgent`, which the title does not mention. The design is smaller and fits the repository. One blocker: an agent bug in one attempt stops every concurrent `ManagedAgent` attempt. Decide the merge order with #10190 before landing.

### System
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph tc["taskcompendium"]
    T["TaskSpec"]
  end
  subgraph re["rolloutengine"]
    RS["RolloutSpec + RolloutLimits"]:::added
    MA["ManagedAgent"]:::added
    E["RolloutEngine"]:::changed
    H["Harness registry"]:::added
    SH["shell_harness"]:::added
    AH["agent_harness"]:::added
    G["_grade_rollout"]:::changed
    C["check_spec"]:::added
  end
  T --> RS
  MA -->|"run(spec, model)"| E
  RS -->|"harness name"| E
  E -->|"check before machines"| C
  E -->|"open / advance / close"| H
  H --> SH
  H --> AH
  E -->|"non-SessionGrader tasks"| G
  classDef changed fill:#fde7c8,stroke:#e8710a,stroke-width:2px
  classDef added fill:#d7f0dd,stroke:#1e8e3e,stroke-width:2px
```

### Why
#10165 asks for `ManagedAgent`: an engine plus a spec that can run a swarm of harness-and-model attempts on arbitrary work, with an optional grader. #10187 asks for a profile of the per-turn trace copy and a rename of `factories`/`sessions`. The diff names the result "prototype G" of a design study in the shared work log (entry 4376). The study also lists bugs on main: grader input checks run only in the built-in session, a server-owned request is never answered at a limit, and cancellation raises `InvalidStateError`.

### Current state
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  L["lower_task"] --> LS["LoweredTaskSpec(task, runtime, session)"]
  LS --> E["RolloutEngine(model, factories, sessions, providers)"]
  E --> S["_ShellboxTaskSession (built in)"]
  E --> F["TaskSessionFactory registry"]
  F --> A["AgentTaskSession"]
```
`RolloutEngine` takes the model at construction, so one engine serves one policy. `LoweredTaskSpec` nests `TaskRuntimeSpec` (machines) and `TaskSessionSpec` (session name, shell options, limits, trace). `validate_lowered_task` returns early for any session other than the built-in `"shellbox"`. Thus custom sessions skip the workspace, resource, and artifact checks. The shell options and the tool providers sit on the spec and the engine. A session grades through a `TaskGrader` callback, and `Transition` carries rewards, token credit, `next_options`, and `reset_conversation`. #9623 added the API on 2026-10-07 and #10054 added `AgentTaskSession` on 2026-10-13. MarinSkyRL uses it in about 40 files, pinned at `23a7a6c2`, a commit on the unmerged branch of #10190.

### How
**A harness is a record of three functions, selected by name per spec.**
```python
# lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/harness.py
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Harness[E: Episode]:
    open: Callable[[HarnessContext], E]
    check: Callable[[RolloutSpec], None] = accept
    grade: Callable[[E, RolloutData], Awaitable[GradeResult]] | None = None
```

**The engine grades every task, except that a `SessionGrader` task needs a harness `grade`.** A harness can no longer override a declared grader.
```python
# lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/engine.py
check_spec(spec, self.machine_factories)
...
if isinstance(spec.task.grader, SessionGrader) and harness.grade is None:
    raise ValueError(...)
harness.check(spec)
```
`check_spec` now applies the workspace checks to every harness, which removes the shellbox-only early return.

**`Transition` keeps only what the engine reads; rewards move to opaque `data`.**
```diff
-    reset_conversation: tuple[dict[str, Any], ...] | None = None
-    reward: float | None = None
-    token_rewards: tuple[float, ...] | None = None
-    next_options: dict[str, Any] | None = None
-    next_prompt_token_ids: tuple[int, ...] | None = None
+    token_ids: tuple[int, ...] | None = None
+    reset: Prompt | None = None
+    data: object = None
```

**The model moves from the constructor to `run(spec, model)`, and the shell options move into `shell_harness(command_timeout=..., shell_tool=..., tools=...)`.** One engine can register several shell configurations.

**The agent bridge treats an identical prompt as a retry and marks undelivered turns with `turn_undelivered`.** `close` fails an open request with `RolloutEnded`.

`ManagedAgent` admits at most `concurrency` attempts and starts the next attempt after the caller takes an outcome. The token trace grows lists and builds tuples on read. The PR states a 29–53% drop in engine time per turn. At head, 161 rolloutengine tests pass locally (except `test_local_grading.py`, which needs bubblewrap), and pyrefly reports 0 errors.

### Limitations
- **Token reward alignment:** `trace.check_transition` is deleted. Misaligned per-token rewards in `Transition.data` now pass silently, and each trainer must check lengths against `response_end`.
- **Undelivered turns:** they are marked, not retracted, so a trainer that ignores `turn_undelivered` trains on a turn that the agent never saw.
- **Performance evidence:** no benchmark is checked in, and nothing posts the profile to #10187, which that issue requires.
- **MarinSkyRL port:** not started. It must rebuild stored Parquet files that hold `LoweredTaskSpec` JSON.

### Review

**Blockers**
1. `lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/agent.py:108` An agent that sends two requests at once after its first turn raises `RolloutContractError`. `advance` re-raises it (`engine.py:355`), and `ManagedAgent._attempt` re-raises it (`managed.py:94-96`), which cancels every concurrent attempt and loses all outcomes and the record of the failing attempt. A probe with three agent specs at `concurrency=3`, one of them calling `complete` twice under `asyncio.gather`, stopped the run with no outcomes. The same error during `prepare` only interrupts its own attempt, so the result depends on timing. This contradicts the body's "a failed attempt does not stop the others". Raise a per-attempt error (not `RolloutContractError`) for agent misuse at `agent.py:108` and `agent.py:129`. Keep `RolloutContractError` for the transport and trace checks (`engine.py:327`, `_Record.add_turn`, `_ExactTokenTrace.append`).

**Related PRs**
2. #10190: MarinSkyRL pins its unmerged branch (`23a7a6c2`), and it edits `agent_session.py`, which this PR deletes, and imports `LoweredTaskSpec`. Land #10190 first, then fold its `agent_session.py` change into `agent.py` here, so that MarinSkyRL can move its pin to main before it ports.
3. #10078, #9799, #10115, #9838, #9839 build on `TaskSession`, `SessionStart`, or `LoweredTaskSpec`, and each needs a port after this lands. #10032, #10045, #10066, #9749, #9626, #9544, #9614, #9766 conflict only in text or docs. None duplicates or deletes what this PR adds.

🤖 Status of this review's points at head cb23ee84f:

- `ManagedAgent` is no longer in this PR (2d4edcd2d), so the blocker about concurrent `ManagedAgent` attempts does not apply here.
- The agent-misuse part did apply: two open requests raised `RolloutContractError` from `advance`, but the same misuse in `prepare` became `RolloutInterrupted`. Since cb23ee84f, the bridge raises `RuntimeError`, and the attempt ends as `RolloutInterrupted` with its record in both places. `RolloutContractError` now means only a token-contract violation. `test_an_agent_with_two_open_requests_ends_only_its_own_attempt` covers this.
- The merge order with #10190 is still open.

topics.title: Cache small FineStore tables within each snapshot view
topics.body:
Reuse immutable Parquet shard bytes across reads of small tables in
`ReadView`. The Atlas grading import made 438 keyed scans across three
GCP metadata tables totaling 6.8 MB. Each scan reopened the same shards;
individual assessment lookups took 7–14 seconds.

Tables other than blob tables can use an automatic cache when their
active shards total at most 8 MiB. Each view has a configurable 64 MiB
budget and reserves a table's full stored size before concurrent readers
fetch its shards. The cache holds compressed bytes; projection,
deduplication, filtering, and streaming stay in the existing reader.
Larger tables and blob tables retain their existing read paths. Cache
lifetime follows the pinned snapshot, so a new view observes later
commits.

With the shared cache, 146 standard assessment lookups over the same 19
shards completed in 8.17 seconds after a 3.14-second cold read. Atlas
uses its existing catalog and loader APIs without a client cache.

The related Atlas data incident is recorded in
[Echo](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/734).
topics.head: c8a424e3d5589449196566715548f8f82dc6c853

comments.body:
🤖 Code review

No issues found.

<!-- marin-correctness-review -->

🤖 Holistic review of c8a424e3d5589449196566715548f8f82dc6c853.

> **In short:** `ReadView` now keeps the compressed Parquet bytes of each non-blob table of at most 8 MiB in memory for the life of the view, under a 64 MiB per-view budget. Larger tables and blob tables use the same paths as before. I found no defects. The one choice to confirm is the per-view budget: views that live a long time keep their cached bytes until they are dropped.

### System
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph finestore["finestore.reader"]
    rv["ReadView._filesystem"]:::changed -->|"non-blob table, size <= min(8 MiB, budget left)"| crh["_CachedReadHandler"]:::added
    rv -->|"otherwise"| base["_ReadOperations._filesystem"]:::added
    base --> fsh["FSSpecHandler / _NoReadAheadHandler"]
    plan["_ReadOperations._read_plan"]:::changed --> rv
    plan --> scan["_read_plan / _scan_plan / iter_shard_rows"]
  end
  crh -->|"one full GET per shard, read once"| store[("object storage")]
  fsh -->|"footer and range reads on every query"| store
  callers["CurationCatalog, evaldash, lm_eval_samples"] --> plan
  classDef changed fill:#fde7c8,stroke:#e8710a,stroke-width:2px
  classDef added fill:#d7f0dd,stroke:#1e8e3e,stroke-width:2px
```

### Why
The PR states that the Atlas grading import ran 438 keyed scans over three GCP metadata tables (6.8 MB in total). Each scan opened the same shards again, and a single assessment lookup took 7–14 seconds. The incident is recorded in Echo wiki/734.

### Current state
Every `scan`, `point`, `iter_rows`, and `keys` call on a view goes through `_ReadOperations._read_plan`. Before this change, that method created a new fsspec filesystem on every call and ran `pq.read_schema` on every active shard, so each query paid at least one footer round trip per shard. The schema scan and the data scan then made further range reads. `ReadView` already pins one immutable manifest, and the manifest records each shard's path and `size_bytes`. The reader did not use those facts to reuse bytes between queries. Long-lived callers such as `CurationCatalog` (`lib/finestore/src/finestore/rl/curation.py:246`) keep one view and query it many times, so they paid the storage latency on every lookup.

### How
**The cache keys on the pinned manifest, so the snapshot decides the cache lifetime.** `_CachedReadHandler` answers `get_file_info` from the manifest sizes without contacting storage. On first open it reads each shard in one request and checks the byte count against the manifest:

```python
# lib/finestore/src/finestore/reader.py:118
with self.fs.open(path, mode="rb", cache_type="none") as source:
    data = source.read(size + 1)
if len(data) != size:
    raise ValueError(f"shard {path!r} has {len(data)} bytes; manifest declares {size}")
```

**Admission reserves the whole table's stored size under the view lock before any bytes arrive.** `ReadView._filesystem` (`reader.py:788`) memoizes one `PyFileSystem` per table. It chooses the cached handler only when the table is not a blob table and `0 < size <= min(_SMALL_TABLE_BYTES, _cache_remaining)`. It subtracts the size from the remaining budget at that point. Concurrent first reads therefore cannot exceed the budget, and a single handler lock ensures each shard is downloaded once.

**The decoding path is unchanged.** The cache stores compressed bytes. Projection, row-group filters, deduplication, and streaming run in the same code as before. The base `_ReadOperations._filesystem` holds the previous handler selection unchanged, so `LegacyReadView` behaves as it did.

`ReadView` gains a keyword `cache_bytes`; zero disables the cache. No caller in the repository passes it except the tests. Two tests use a byte-counting fsspec filesystem. The first checks that four concurrent cold lookups and several later query shapes fetch exactly the table's stored bytes, and that a newer view sees later commits. The second checks the shared budget and `cache_bytes=0`. I ran `lib/finestore/tests` at head: 116 passed.

### Limitations
- **Evidence:** The figures of 8.17 s for 146 warm lookups and 3.14 s for the cold read come from the PR body. No benchmark or log is attached.
- **Footprint per view:** The budget applies to each view, not to the process. A long-lived view such as `CurationCatalog.view` holds up to 64 MiB until it is dropped, and a process with N live views can hold N × 64 MiB.
- **One-shot views read whole tables:** The first `keys()`, `schema_version`, or `point` call on a small table now fetches the full table, up to 8 MiB, where it used to fetch only footers and column chunks. This affects callers such as `lm_eval_samples.py:954` that create a view for a single query.
- **Serial cold fill:** `_read_plan` calls `pq.read_schema` on the shards one after another, so the first query downloads the shards serially. The handler lock also makes concurrent first reads of different shards wait for each other.

### Review

No findings.

The affected-test run failed on evaluation row ordering and a terminated Levanter worker, then timed out; both failed tests passed when rerun alone. I did not commit or push.

topics.title: Publish a stable Atlas catalog with FineStore range caching
topics.body:
Publish production FULL campaigns directly to `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/catalog/production` with an explicit `--publish-catalog` option. Keep reports and artifacts versioned, and keep local and SAMPLE catalogs separate. Seed the stable catalog with the existing 206 source declarations, 146 assessments and 12,107 judgments with evidence packets. Retain its immutable shards in the verified archive at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/migrations/2026-10-15/`.

Accumulate selected sources while preserving unselected entries and their pinned dataset and pipeline declarations, including IDs absent from an older checkout. Ignore superseded attempts per source using retained campaign start times. Assessment keys include dataset revisions, pipeline dependencies, rubric and model identity: a failed changed-key assessment clears the old grade, while an exact-key retry can reuse completed evidence. Check publication-lease ownership and the starting catalog pointer before selecting a catalog snapshot.

Default Atlas imports to the stable root. Keep Postgres refresh explicit and retryable, with a conditional serving-pointer update. Cleanup deletes rows for load IDs observed before staging and always excludes the currently served load. Reject imports whose source catalog changed while loading. Grading, curriculum publication and Marina deployments remain separate operations.

Replace FineStore's whole-shard cache admission with an LRU of requested Parquet byte ranges. Each `ReadView` owns a configurable 64 MiB budget shared across tables. Table and shard sizes do not determine admission; reads larger than the budget bypass it. Fetch misses with ranged reads, charge GCS transfer budgets for the requested bytes, and reject short reads before caching. Blob decoding and Atlas evidence reads retain their batch limits.

On the GCP assessment table's 19 shards, a 3.40-second cold scan warmed the view's cache; all 146 subsequent source point lookups took 4.31 seconds in total. Without reader caching, three individual source lookups on the same table took 7.03, 7.10 and 14.19 seconds.

Builds on #10207. The [Atlas incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/734) tracks catalog selection, bootstrap and the production import.

🤖 Code review

No issues found.

<!-- marin-correctness-review -->

🤖 Holistic review of 0d8e82ffabb1b5bea8977421898f5bb5f1d53a51.

> **In short:** This PR replaces #10207's whole-shard small-table cache in `ReadView` with one per-view LRU of the Parquet byte ranges that Arrow requests. Every table goes through it, blob tables included. It also gives the Atlas loader a default catalog root. The cache design holds up. Two things need a decision: `--catalog-root` now has a silent default, and the new cache dropped the shard-size check.

### System
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph atlas["Atlas loader (infra/marina)"]
    main["load.py main: --catalog-root"]:::changed --> lc["load_catalog"]
    lc --> cc["CurationCatalog"]
  end
  subgraph fs["FineStore reader"]
    cc -->|"point / scan / read_blobs"| rv["ReadView._filesystem"]:::changed
    rv -->|"one per view, all tables"| h["_CachedReadHandler"]:::changed
    h --> f["_CachedReadFile"]:::added
    f -->|"_fetch_range"| c["_ReadRangeCache (LRU, 64 MiB)"]:::added
    c -->|"miss: cache_type=none"| obj["fsspec object storage"]
  end
  classDef changed fill:#fde7c8,stroke:#e8710a,stroke-width:2px
  classDef added fill:#d7f0dd,stroke:#1e8e3e,stroke-width:2px
```

### Why
The Atlas grading import made 438 keyed scans over three small metadata tables. Before any caching, each `point` reopened the same shards, and the PR states that three lookups took 7.03, 7.10 and 14.19 s. #10207 added a cache for whole small tables. This PR replaces it with a range cache so that tables over 8 MiB also benefit. It also points production imports at the relocated catalog in `s3://marin-us-east-02a` ([Echo wiki/734](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/734)).

### Current state
At the merge base (`3950f51ccb`), `ReadView._filesystem(table)` gave each table its own `PyFileSystem`. A non-blob table whose shards totaled at most 8 MiB, and that still fit in the view's remaining 64 MiB, got a `_CachedReadHandler`. That handler read each whole shard once, checked the length against `Shard.size_bytes`, and served `pa.BufferReader`s. Larger tables used plain `FSSpecHandler`. Blob tables (`DESCRIPTORS`, `PARTS`) used `_NoReadAheadHandler`, which skips fsspec's 50 MiB read-ahead. The loader required `--catalog-root`. What was missing: point lookups on tables over 8 MiB still went back to storage every time, and budget reserved by one table could never be reclaimed.

### How
**A view owns one byte-range LRU, shared by all shard handles across all tables.** `_filesystem` now ignores `table` whenever `cache_bytes > 0`:
```python
# lib/finestore/src/finestore/reader.py:826
if self._read_filesystem is None:
    fs, _ = factory.url_to_fs(self.root)
    shards = [shard for state in self._snapshot.manifest.tables.values() for shard in state.shards]
    self._read_filesystem = PyFileSystem(_CachedReadHandler(fs, shards, self._cache_bytes))
```
**A lookup hits only when one cached range contains the request.** A miss takes a per-path lock, fetches exactly `[start, end)` with `cache_type="none"`, then evicts from the LRU head until the new range fits. A read larger than the budget is returned without being admitted. Partial overlaps are fetched again and stored as separate entries.

**Blob tables now share the cache.** `_blob_descriptors` calls `self._filesystem(BlobTables.DESCRIPTORS)` (`reader.py:751`) and no longer builds its own `_NoReadAheadHandler`. Because `_CachedReadFile` reads with `cache_type="none"`, blob reads still skip read-ahead. `test_blob_lookup_avoids_remote_readahead_of_unmatched_row_groups` still passes through this path.

**The loader defaults `--catalog-root` to `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/catalog/legacy-2026-10-12`** (`load.py:20`). The documented command drops the flag.

Tests: the existing reuse/snapshot and shared-budget tests were rewritten for LRU eviction, and a new test reads selected row groups from a shard twice the budget. Locally, `lib/finestore/tests` passes (117). `infra/marina/tests/test_rl_data_catalog.py` timed out starting local Postgres on this VM, so the loader tests are unverified here. The timing numbers in the body come from the author's runs. No artifact in the diff backs them.

### Limitations
- **Blob payloads compete with metadata:** chunked blob part ranges under 64 MiB are admitted to the same LRU, so a long-lived view that interleaves `read_blobs` with point lookups evicts the footers it reuses. Atlas reads packets after metadata, so it is not affected.
- **Lookup cost:** each read scans every cached range for its path while holding the view-wide lock. That is fine at today's range counts and grows linearly with them.
- **Same-shard misses serialize:** a miss holds `_file_locks[path]` for the whole remote fetch, including bypassed oversized reads, so a concurrent hit on that shard waits.

### Review

**Should fix**
1. `infra/marina/applets/rl_data_catalog/load.py:195` The silent default turns `load.py --applet-id ...` into "select the 2026-10-12 catalog". `load_catalog` skips only when `(catalog_root, snapshot_id)` matches what Atlas currently serves (`load.py:84`). If production later moves to another root, running the documented command without the flag silently replaces production with this dated snapshot. AGENTS.md requires explicit specification of critical parameters. Keep `required=True` and put the canonical root in the documented command at `docs/references/rl-data-atlas.md:99`. Alternatively, have the loader refuse a root that differs from the selected load's `catalog_root` unless an explicit flag allows it.
2. `lib/finestore/src/finestore/reader.py:125` The range cache does not check `len(data) == end - start`. #10207 raised `ValueError("shard ... has N bytes; manifest declares M")`. Now a short read, such as a manifest size larger than the object or a truncated response, is cached under the full `(start, end)` key. Every later read inside that range returns truncated bytes for the life of the view, and Arrow reports a Parquet decode error with no shard context. Raise before admission: `if len(data) != end - start: raise ValueError(f"shard {path!r}: read {len(data)} of {end - start} bytes at {start}")`.

**Related PRs**
3. #9934, #9881, #9695: each edits other sections of `docs/references/rl-data-atlas.md` (source registration and review invalidation). They are independent of this PR and can merge in either order.

<!-- marin-holistic-review:0d8e82ffabb1b5bea8977421898f5bb5f1d53a51 -->

🤖 Removed the inaccurate README sentence about new views loading the current manifest and corrected the loader docstring for alternate catalog roots. FineStore cache tests: 19 passed; changed-file lint passed.

topics.title: [finestore] Cut object-store requests per flush and lookup, elect one maintainer, add a simulated S3 backend
topics.body:
FineStore writers sharing one archive spent most of their object-store requests on rename staging, re-reading HEAD before every commit, and compactions that lost the HEAD race. This change adds a simulated S3 backend to measure that, then cuts the request count and elects one compactor per archive.

**Commit path.** Remote shards are uploaded straight to their final key instead of staged and renamed. A commit starts from the manifest this writer last published, so an uncontended flush reads nothing before its compare-and-swap. A lost compare-and-swap re-reads HEAD, rebases, and retries after a backoff from 0.5 s to 5 s for up to an hour of wall time, so a flush does not fail under many writers. A one-row flush now costs three requests instead of eight; a read view costs two instead of three because a populated archive is validated from HEAD alone.

**Maintenance.** One writer per archive compacts at a time. The maintenance pass takes a lease at `_maintenance` under the root and publishes a manifest with the next `maintainer_epoch`; compaction commits carry the epoch they were prepared under and are rejected once a later maintainer announces itself. The lease is refreshed on a heartbeat while compactions run. Writers without the lease flush and leave compaction to the holder. The close-time merge is best effort: a closing writer that holds the lease, or can take a free or stale one, merges every writer's level-zero shards within the close budget, and a closer that finds another writer maintaining the archive leaves its shards to that writer. A wave of closing writers therefore elects one merger instead of racing replacement commits. A writer from an older FineStore build compacts without the lease and carries the epoch forward unchanged.

**Lookups.** Each shard records its smallest and largest primary key when keys are strings and integers. Lookups with `==` on a key prefix, or `in` on the first key column, skip shards whose bounds exclude the value, including blob descriptor reads. Shard schemas are cached per process, and manifest shards are opened without the existence check Arrow's fsspec handler issues first.

**Simulator.** `finestore.testing.simulated_s3` is an in-memory `s3://` filesystem that charges one round trip per request, serves ranged reads one block at a time, implements rename as COPY plus DELETE, and fails overlapping conditional writes the way S3 does. It records every request, so tests pin request budgets and `lib/finestore/scripts/benchmark_multi_writer.py` compares commit strategies without a bucket. The FineStore suite runs 64 behaviour tests on both a local root and the simulated backend. The benchmark also takes `--root` to drive the same writers against real storage.

Commit, conflict, compaction, abandonment, and lease counters are exported as `finestore_*` telemetry.

**Simulator benchmark**, 100 ms per request at time scale 0.1 (elapsed is raw at that scale; CPU work is not compressed), 8 flushes of 64 rows per writer:

| writers, layout | elapsed s before → after | requests | compactions (abandoned) | final shards | point lookup requests |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 16, shared root | 21.9 → 10.7 | 6737 → 1811 | 49 (30) → 2 (0) | 7 → 2 | 32 → 4 |
| 16, shared root, no maintenance | 12.2 → 7.6 | 2384 → 1947 | 16 (0) → 16 (0) | 16 → 16 | 68 → 5 |
| 16, per-writer roots | 4.9 → 3.2 | 1872 → 1246 | 16 (0) → 16 (0) | 16 → 16 | 8 → 5 |
| 64, shared root, 4 flushes, scale 0.05 | 82.8 → 14.6 | 23331 → 8504 | 198 (130) → 2 (0) | 10 → 2 | 44 → 4 |

Before the backoff change, a 50 ms initial retry drove 64 writers to about 29 conflicts per commit and 33k requests; the 0.5 s start cut that to 11k with no loss in elapsed time, and electing one closer to merge cut it to 8.5k with no abandoned compactions.

**GCS from an Iris job in the bucket's region** (`--root temp`, 8 flushes of 64 rows per writer; request counts are not observable there):

| writers, layout | elapsed s before → after | compactions (abandoned) | final shards | point lookup s |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1, shared root | 9.6 → 5.7 | 1 (0) → 1 (0) | 1 → 1 | 0.30 → 0.18 |
| 4, shared root | 25.8 → 23.7 | 5 (1) → 4 (0) | 5 → 4 | 0.82 → 0.18 |
| 16, shared root | 162.3 → 76.3 | 41 (23) → 2 (0) | 6 → 2 | 1.07 → 0.18 |
| 16, shared root, no maintenance | 93.8 → 72.5 | 16 (0) → 16 (2) | 16 → 30 | 2.11 → 0.24 |
| 16, per-writer roots | 10.1 → 7.8 | 16 (0) → 16 (0) | 16 → 16 | 0.26 → 0.18 |
| 64, shared root, 4 flushes | 473.8 → 141.5 | 125 (81) → 3 (1) | 5 → 2 | 1.50 → 0.17 |

A shared root still commits at a fixed rate of roughly 1.5 flushes per second, so each writer's flush latency grows linearly with the number of writers; per-writer roots scale out. That serialization is inherent to one compare-and-swapped HEAD and is what the proposal's per-writer logs address. The 16- and 64-writer rows are from the elected close merge; the other rows predate it. On GCS the 64 writers saw 1078 commit retries and the 16 writers 168, counted from the retry log.

These measurements back the FineStore concurrency proposal in Loom session bth4qn4d (artifact `finestore-improvements`): this is its P1; per-writer logs and the key side table remain proposed.

### Why
FineStore tests ran only against local disk, where every request is free and the commit pointer uses `flock`. The behaviour that matters on object storage, such as round trips per flush, rename as COPY plus DELETE, and HEAD contention between writers, was not measured. The PR states that the benchmark numbers support the concurrency proposal in Loom session bth4qn4d (shared root: 281 s and 6773 requests; per-writer roots: 56 s and 2079 requests).

### Current state
`DataStore` resolves storage through `rigging.filesystem.factory.url_to_fs`/`open_url` and `StoragePath`, writes shards through `atomic_rename`, and publishes commits with compare-and-swap on HEAD through `rigging.filesystem.conditional_object.conditional_object`. That function dispatches to the Local, Gcs, or S3 `ConditionalObject`. `finestore.commit` and `finestore.migrations.m0001_manifest` each import `conditional_object` by name. Commit retries go through `rigging.timing.retry_with_backoff`, which calls `time.sleep`. `test_finestore.py` contains a single `MemoryFileSystem` fixture and nothing that measures request cost.

### How
**A process-wide context manager routes every `s3://` access to one private `MemoryFileSystem` subclass that charges latency and records each request.**
```python
# lib/finestore/src/finestore/simulated_s3.py
with (
    mock.patch.object(factory, "url_to_fs", url_to_fs),
    mock.patch.object(factory, "open_url", open_url),
    mock.patch.object(finestore.commit, "conditional_object", lambda path: SimulatedConditionalObject(path, fs)),
    mock.patch("rigging.timing.time.sleep", scaled_sleep),
):
    yield fs
```
**HEAD compare-and-swap models the S3 409.** A conditional write that starts while another conditional write on the same key is in flight fails with `ConditionalRequestConflict`. Otherwise an ETag mismatch fails with `PreconditionFailed`. Only the later of two overlapping writes fails; the PR body states this.

**Ranged reads cost one GET per uncached block.** `_BlockReader` honours `cache_type="none"` and `block_size`, which `reader.py:85,95` pass to `fs.open`.

**The `archive_root` fixture runs each test twice, once on local disk and once on `s3://finestore-tests/run` with zero latency.** Tests that read Parquet directly now use `_parquet_metadata`/`_read_parquet`, which open through `StoragePath`.

Evidence: `uv run --package marin-finestore pytest lib/finestore/tests` passes 188 tests in 27 s. 64 of the 77 tests in `test_finestore.py` take `archive_root`. The budget tests pin a one-row flush at 8 requests or fewer and a `ReadView` open at 3 or fewer. I did not rerun the benchmark numbers in the body.

### Limitations
- **Migrations stay local-only:** all `migrat*`/legacy tests still use `tmp_path`, so the v1→v2 path never runs on the simulated backend (see item 2).
- **Maintenance backoff is unscaled:** `store.py:455` waits on `self._stop.wait(delay)`, which `time_scale` does not compress. Benchmark runs that hit transient maintenance failures report inflated wall times.
- **Cost model only:** CPU time is not scaled, `version()` is charged as a GET where real S3 uses HEAD, and the 409 rule never fails both writers.
- **No review threads yet:** Codex review was still running at this head.

### Review

**Should fix**
1. `lib/finestore/src/finestore/simulated_s3.py:22` Test machinery ships in the `marin-finestore` wheel. The module imports `unittest.mock` and patches `rigging` module attributes on use, and nothing in `src` calls it. Other packages keep this in a `testing` subpackage: `iris.testing`, `zephyr.testing`, `levanter.testing`. Move it to `finestore/testing/simulated_s3.py`, or `finestore/testing.py`, and update the conftest, test, and benchmark imports.
2. `lib/finestore/src/finestore/simulated_s3.py:371` Only `finestore.commit.conditional_object` is patched. `finestore/migrations/m0001_manifest.py:15` binds its own `conditional_object`, so `migrate()` and `migrate_for_write` on an `s3://` root under `simulated_s3()` build a real boto `S3ConditionalObject` for ARCHIVE/HEAD, while the payload reads and writes go to the fake. The result is real-bucket calls, or credential errors, from a "simulated" test. Also patch `finestore.migrations.m0001_manifest.conditional_object`, or have m0001 call `finestore.commit.conditional_object` through the module, and move the migration tests onto `archive_root`.
3. `lib/finestore/src/finestore/simulated_s3.py:372` `rigging.timing.time` is the stdlib `time` module, so `mock.patch("rigging.timing.time.sleep", ...)` replaces `time.sleep` for every module and thread in the process. That includes pytest plugins, Arrow I/O callers, and any other library sleeping during `test_concurrent_writers_publish_every_row_through_conflicts` at `time_scale=0.001`. The comment at `:35` says the patch scales FineStore's retry backoff only. Scope it to rigging's retry loop: `mock.patch.object(rigging.timing, "time", SimpleNamespace(sleep=scaled_sleep, monotonic=time.monotonic, time=time.time))`, adding any other `time.*` names `rigging.timing` uses.

**Tests to drop**
4. `test_rename_costs_a_copy_and_a_delete` (`lib/finestore/tests/test_simulated_s3.py:42`): reimplementation. It asserts that `SimulatedS3.mv`, defined at `simulated_s3.py:253` as `cp_file` plus `rm`, records one COPY and one DELETE. It fails only when the fake changes, never when FineStore does. The flush budget test already covers rename cost through `atomic_rename`.

**Related PRs**
5. #10208 (Atlas catalog range caching) edits `lib/finestore/src/finestore/reader.py` and `test_cache.py`, with no file overlap. Its range-caching changes can move the `ReadView` request count that `test_read_view_costs_three_requests` pins. They can land in either order. Whichever lands second should rebase and rerun the budget tests.

<!-- marin-holistic-review:e50c4fd157b989a5a2d3f502274e403b3e3af563 -->

🤖 Removed the simulator-only rename test and redundant ReadView token assertion; clarified the simulator docstring and sleep comment. FineStore tests: 187 passed. Changed-files lint passed.

<!-- marin-deslop:e50c4fd157b989a5a2d3f502274e403b3e3af563 -->

🤖 Holistic review of 27a2dafddb61fb295f40dd573e7a01536d09f944.

> **In short:** The PR now changes the FineStore commit protocol as well as adding the simulator. It writes shards straight to their final key, starts each commit from the last published snapshot, shortens the commit backoff, and adds a lease-elected maintainer with a manifest epoch. Two blockers: at 64 writers a flush now raises `CommitConflict`, and compactions longer than 90 s cannot publish.

### System
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph fs["finestore"]
    ds["DataStore maintain/seal/close"]:::changed
    cc["CommitCoordinator commit/last_snapshot"]:::changed
    comp["compaction._compact_shards"]:::changed
    sw["ShardWriter"]:::changed
    rv["ReadView / read_snapshot"]:::changed
    man["Manifest.maintainer_epoch"]:::added
    sim["simulated_s3"]:::added
  end
  subgraph rig["rigging"]
    lease["distributed_lock S3Lease root/_maintenance"]
    cas["conditional_object"]
  end
  ds -- "try_acquire / refresh" --> lease
  ds -- "epoch_update" --> cc
  comp -- "expected_epoch" --> cc
  cc -- "CAS HEAD" --> cas
  cc --> man
  ds --> sw
  sim -- "patches" --> cas
  classDef changed fill:#fde7c8,stroke:#e8710a,stroke-width:2px
  classDef added fill:#d7f0dd,stroke:#1e8e3e,stroke-width:2px
```

### Why
The previous head measured what FineStore costs on object storage. A one-row flush took 8 requests, and with 16 writers on a shared root 44 of 61 compactions were abandoned after losing the HEAD race. Commit 27a2dafddb implements the "request diet" and "lease-elected maintainer" parts of the proposal in Loom session bth4qn4d.

### Current state
At e50c4fd157 every writer compacted from its maintenance thread and on close. `ShardWriter` staged each shard to a temp sibling and renamed it, which on S3 costs PUT, COPY, DELETE, and HEADs. `CommitCoordinator.commit` read HEAD before every compare-and-swap and retried up to 32 times with backoff from 1 s up to 10 min. `ReadView` read the `_archive.json` marker before HEAD. Nothing elected a compactor, so concurrent writers duplicated merges and threw them away.

### How
**Only the holder of a `root/_maintenance` lease compacts during `maintain()` and close, and acquiring the lease publishes a new `maintainer_epoch`.**
```python
# lib/finestore/src/finestore/commit.py (_apply_delta)
if delta.expected_epoch is not None and base.maintainer_epoch != delta.expected_epoch:
    raise CommitConflict(...)
if delta.epoch_update is not None and delta.epoch_update <= base.maintainer_epoch:
    raise CommitConflict(...)
```
`_compact_shards` passes `expected_epoch` from its base snapshot, so a compaction prepared before a takeover is rejected. `seal()` still compacts without the lease.

**A commit with no explicit base starts from the snapshot this coordinator last published.** A stale base costs one lost compare-and-swap, then the existing refresh path rebases it.

**A lost compare-and-swap now retries after 50 ms, capped at 2 s, still for 32 attempts.**

**Remote shards are uploaded to their final key.** Local shards keep the `atomic_rename` path. `read_snapshot` reads the format marker only when HEAD is absent.

Mechanical changes: the PR adds commit, conflict, compaction, and lease telemetry counters. `simulated_s3` now also patches `distributed_lock.conditional_object`, and its `cp_file` no longer sleeps while holding the store lock. The deslop commit removed the rename test.

Evidence: 192 tests pass locally, including `test_only_the_maintenance_lease_holder_compacts` and `test_compaction_prepared_under_an_older_epoch_is_rejected`. The budget tests now pin a flush at 3 requests or fewer and a read view at 2 or fewer.

### Limitations
- **Mixed-version fleets:** older writers keep `maintainer_epoch` (`extra="allow"`) but compact without the lease or the epoch check.
- **Simulator `pipe_file`:** the loom-oa-dev thread at `simulated_s3.py:268` still applies. `_open` ignores `data=`, so piped objects are stored empty.
- **Simulator protocol:** the Codex thread at `simulated_s3.py:183` still applies. The `memory` protocol rewrites `ls`/`glob` results to `memory://`.
- **Benchmark clock:** the lease timeout reads `time.time()`, which `time_scale` does not compress. Lease behaviour in scaled runs does not match production.
- **Description:** the body still states 8 and 3 requests and describes only the simulator (item 9).

### Review

**Carried from e50c4fd157**
- 1: open. `simulated_s3.py` still ships in `src/finestore` instead of a `finestore/testing` package.
- 2: open. `m0001_manifest.py:15` still binds an unpatched `conditional_object`. This head adds a `distributed_lock` patch but not this one.
- 3: changed. The comment at `simulated_s3.py:35` now says the patch replaces the stdlib function, but `time.sleep` is still replaced for the whole process at `:373`.
- 4: resolved. The deslop commit 6c7f73c319 removed `test_rename_costs_a_copy_and_a_delete`.
- 5: open. See item 10.

**Blockers**
6. `lib/finestore/src/finestore/commit.py:36` Lowering the backoff cap from 10 min to 2 s, with the same 32 attempts, gives a writer about 60 s of patience, and high writer counts exhaust it. I ran `benchmark_multi_writer.py --writers 64 --commits 4 --time-scale 0.05`. At this head a writer's `store.flush()` raised `CommitConflict: HEAD at s3://bench/archive changed 32 consecutive times`. At e50c4fd157 the same run finished in 902 s with 717 conflicts. A flush that raises loses the writer. Keep the 50 ms initial delay, but bound the retries by time: pass `max_elapsed=` (for example 600 s) to `retry_with_backoff` with a large `max_attempts`, and add the 64-writer row to the benchmark evidence.
7. `lib/finestore/src/finestore/store.py:390` The lease is refreshed only when `maintain()` starts. `HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT` is 90 s (`distributed_lock.py:39`), and nothing refreshes it while compactions run. If a compaction pass takes longer than 90 s, another writer takes the stale lease and bumps the epoch, and the running compaction is rejected at commit. The new holder's long compaction then loses the same way to the old holder, so with two writers on a shared root a pass longer than 90 s never publishes. At e50c4fd157 such a compaction rebased and published. Wrap the compaction work in `maintain()`, `seal()`, and `close()` in `lease_refresh(self._lease)` (`distributed_lock.py:186`), which already runs a heartbeat thread for this purpose.

**Should fix**
8. `lib/finestore/src/finestore/store.py:383` Nothing synchronizes `_acquire_maintenance`. It runs on the maintenance thread through `maintain()` and on the caller's thread through `seal()` and public `maintain()`. Two concurrent calls in one store both pass `try_acquire` (same `worker_id`) and both propose epoch e+1. The loser's `CommitConflict` branch then calls `self._lease.release()`, which deletes the lease the winner just took, so the winner's next `refresh()` raises `LeaseLostError`. Guard the lease state with its own `threading.Lock`.
9. PR title and body: they describe a test simulator and quote budgets of 8 and 3 requests and benchmark numbers from before 27a2dafddb. The diff now changes the manifest format (`maintainer_epoch`), adds a `_maintenance` object to every root, and changes commit retry and shard upload semantics. Retitle the PR, describe the protocol change and the mixed-version behaviour, and re-measure the benchmark at this head.

**Related PRs**
10. #10208 (Atlas catalog range caching) edits `reader.py` and `test_cache.py`. This PR now edits `ReadView.__init__` in `reader.py` as well and pins its cost at 2 requests. Whichever lands second must rebase over the `ReadView` constructor and rerun `test_read_view_costs_two_requests`.

<!-- marin-holistic-review:27a2dafddb61fb295f40dd573e7a01536d09f944 -->

🤖 Addressed the review of 27a2dafddb in 2897efb216, with the lookup work from 3d2a1a53e1 in between.

- Blocker 6: commit retries are bounded by ten minutes of wall time instead of 32 attempts. The 64-writer row is being re-measured and will go in the description.
- Blocker 7: `maintain()` and `seal()` wrap their compactions in `lease_refresh`, so a pass longer than the lease timeout keeps its lease.
- Item 8: maintenance passes from the background thread and from callers are serialized by a lock, so one pass at a time acquires, refreshes, and releases the lease.
- Carried 1 and 2: the simulator now lives in `finestore.testing.simulated_s3` and patches the migration module's `conditional_object`.
- Carried 3: the comment now says the patch replaces `time.sleep` for the whole process.
- Close-time merging no longer takes the lease. The benchmark showed that gating it left most writers' level-zero shards behind when they closed together; closers touch disjoint inputs, so the merge needs no election.
- Mixed-version behaviour is documented in the README: an older writer compacts without the lease and its commits carry the epoch forward unchanged.
- Item 9: the title and description will be rewritten once the re-measured numbers are in.

topics.title: Update holistic reviews in place and scale their walkthroughs
topics.body:
Holistic re-reviews replace the original overview comment by its exact ID and preserve finding numbers, including after a rebase. New or materially changed actionable findings may also appear in one new top-level PR comment linking to the overview. Separate markers keep that comment out of overview discovery. If editing the overview fails, report the failure without creating a duplicate. This prevents the repeated walkthroughs seen on #10209.

Provide short and full review examples, a Mermaid flowchart example, and explicit create-versus-edit instructions. Self-contained changes use brief prose; larger changes can retain the system, motivation, before/after, design, and limits outline. Use bold labels for short sections and headings where they help navigation, and keep evidence with the finding it supports.
