topics.title: [gpu] Unify the managed GPU stack on CUDA 13 and audit version pins
topics.body:
## Goal

Use a supported PyTorch CUDA 13 build alongside JAX CUDA 13, and keep only the direct version pins that protect a demonstrated compatibility boundary. The uv lock should provide reproducibility; package requirements should use ranges where safe.

## Current blocker

`marin-core[gpu]` currently resolves:

- JAX on CUDA 13 with `nvidia-cublas>=13.2.0.9`.
- PyTorch 2.11 from the cu128 index with separate CUDA 12 runtime packages.

The PyTorch cu130 wheel cannot replace cu128 as-is: it requires `cuda-toolkit[cublas]==13.0.2`, which pins `nvidia-cublas==13.1.0.3` and conflicts with Marin’s B200 cuBLAS floor.

## Work

1. Find a supported PyTorch CUDA 13 resolution that retains Marin’s H100 NCCL and B200 cuBLAS guards. Prefer a newer compatible release over overriding an upstream exact CUDA-library dependency.
2. Audit the direct GPU requirements for `torch`, `torchvision`, and the CUDA libraries:
   - Document why each exact pin or bounded range is necessary.
   - Replace exact application-level pins with compatible ranges where the lockfile and upstream dependency metadata are sufficient.
   - Keep hardware safety floors such as cuBLAS/NCCL until validation proves they are obsolete.
3. Update the PyTorch index selection and uv lock.
4. Validate imports, device execution, matmul, and collectives on H100 and B200; run the existing H100 GPU canary.

## Acceptance criteria

- `marin-core[gpu]` installs one coherent CUDA 13 environment without per-job overrides.
- PyTorch and TorchVision resolve as a compatible pair.
- The resolved cuBLAS and NCCL versions retain the existing B200 and H100 fixes.
- Every remaining direct exact pin has a nearby compatibility rationale; otherwise it is expressed as the narrowest validated range.
- H100 and B200 smoke tests pass, and the H100 GPU canary passes.

<details>
<summary>Why the current constraints exist</summary>

- **Torch 2.11:** selected in #5379 because Torch 2.10 cu128 pinned NCCL 2.27.5, which reproduced a CoreWeave H100 all-to-all failure. Torch 2.11 cu128 brought NCCL 2.28.9, which passed the probe.
- **TorchVision 0.26:** this is the native-extension compatibility pair for Torch 2.11. PR #6346 demonstrated why changing Torch without changing TorchVision is unsafe.
- **cuBLAS floor:** `nvidia-cublas>=13.2.0.9` was added in #5428 after older CUDA 13 builds warned on B200. Marin does not directly exact-pin cuBLAS; uv records the selected version in the lock.
- **cu128 index:** retained because the available Torch cu130 metadata exact-pinned cuBLAS below that B200 floor.
- **vLLM:** the selected vLLM revision also pins its build/runtime Torch and TorchVision pair exactly. Relaxing Marin alone may therefore not be enough for GPU vLLM; any required fork change belongs with #7135.

</details>

Blocks #7135. The downstream `marin-serve --gpu` integration remains tracked by #7111.

topics.title: Easy single-tool-call eval for base models (MCP-Atlas-Easy) — item 3 of #7090
topics.body:
🤖 Picks up **item 3 (arbitrary tool use)** of #7090 — the easy, base-model end of it.

## Dataset

https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/mcp-atlas-easy

**MCP-Atlas-Easy** is a 220-row single-tool-call benchmark for *pretrained (base) models*, derived from [ScaleAI/MCP-Atlas](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ScaleAI/mcp-atlas) (36 real MCP servers, 220 tools, CC-BY-4.0). MCP-Atlas evaluates instruction-tuned agents on multi-step orchestration (3–6 calls per task); this strips the same skill down to its simplest form: **one tool spec, one trivially unambiguous request, one correct tool call, then stop.**

## Format

One row per unique tool. Each row carries structured fields (`tool`, `server`, `description`, `input_schema`, `scenario`, `target_call`) plus ready-to-use `prompt`/`completion` strings:

```
The following is a demonstration of correct tool use. Given a tool
specification and a user request, the assistant responds with a single
JSON tool call.

Tool specification:
{
  "name": "whois_whois_domain",
  "description": "Look up WHOIS registration information for a domain name.",
  "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"domain": {...}}, "required": ["domain"]}
}

User request: Look up WHOIS information for the domain openai.com.

Tool call: {"name": "whois_whois_domain", "arguments": {"domain": "openai.com"}}<|endoftext|>
```

The target completion is the JSON call followed by `<|endoftext|>` (swap for the tokenizer's real EOS when building eval inputs), so it works as a completion-style eval with no chat template and scores two things: **call correctness** (parse the JSON, match against `target_call` / validate against `input_schema`) and **clean stopping** (does the model emit EOS or degenerate into continuation).

## Construction

1. Extracted all 220 unique tool names from MCP-Atlas `ENABLED_TOOLS`, plus per-tool evidence: declared required/optional params (41 tools) and real invocation arguments mined from the `TRAJECTORY` fields (106 tools).
2. Claude Sonnet generated a grounded spec (description + JSON Schema) and one deliberately easy scenario + correct call per tool.
3. Programmatic validation: every target call satisfies its own schema (required args present, no undeclared args); all 220 tools covered exactly once.

## Caveats

- **103/220 schemas are inferred.** Those tools are never called in the public MCP-Atlas trajectories and have no declared params, so schemas were inferred from tool names and known server behavior (e.g. `f1-mcp-server_*`, `anili_*`, most `notion_API-*`). Rows are always internally consistent — the target call matches the spec shown in the prompt — but inferred schemas may not match the real servers' wire formats. Treat as a formatting/grounding eval, not a live-server integration test.
- Scenarios and calls are synthetic (Claude Sonnet), not human-authored.

## Open follow-ups toward the full item 3

- These are real, public MCP servers, so the "unlikely to appear in the pretraining corpus" criterion is only partially met. A follow-up could mutate tool names/schemas (or synthesize novel tools) to guarantee unseen-ness.
- Harder variants: multiple tools in context (selection, not just invocation), optional-arg scenarios, distractor tools, and multi-step composition — bridging back toward full MCP-Atlas difficulty.

topics.title: [iris] Native container customization: add deps/setup on a base image without a custom Dockerfile
topics.body:
## Description

Follow-up from #7233. That PR's TPU eval launcher had to ship a full custom image (`docker/evalchemy-tpu/Dockerfile`) purely to add "extra stuff" — the `marin-community/evalchemy` fork + `lm-eval==0.4.12` + boxed-answer graders + an nltk cache — on top of a known-good base (`ghcr.io/open-thoughts/openthoughts-agent:tpu`, vllm-tpu 0.20.0). @rjpower asked whether Iris could let a user customize a base image *natively* so a full Dockerfile isn't needed for the "just install a few things" case. Custom images stay allowed; this is about the common case.

**How images/deps work today**
- A job's image is `ResourceConfig.image` (`lib/fray/src/fray/types.py:407`), forwarded as `task_image` and pulled/run in `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/runtime/docker.py` (`ensure_image`, then `docker create`). Default is `ghcr.io/marin-community/iris-task:latest` (`lib/iris/config/marin.yaml:48`).
- `remote()` (`lib/marin/src/marin/execution/remote.py:80`) only plumbs `extras` + `env_vars`; it leaves `pip_packages=[]` / `setup_scripts=None`, so Iris always `uv sync`s the marin repo into `/app/.venv` (`setup_scripts.py`, `runtime/env.py:29`), even under a custom image.

**The gap that forced a Dockerfile**
1. `EnvironmentConfig` *does* have `pip_packages` / `setup_scripts` (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/types.py:562`) that render `uv pip install …`, but they always target `/app/.venv` — never the image's baked venv. The eval needs packages in the image's `/opt/openthoughts/.venv` (where vllm-tpu lives), so it must invoke that interpreter explicitly and no native install path can reach it.
2. Neither `pip_packages` nor `setup_scripts` is plumbed through `remote()`, and there is no `--pip` / `--requirement` / `--setup-script` CLI flag (only `--extra` / `--sync-package` / `--task-image`).
3. No apt/system-package hook. Native installs also re-run every submit (re-clone + re-download over the open internet each job — a cost driver AGENTS.md flags), vs. a baked, digest-pinned image that does it once.

**Proposals (pick one)**
1. *Declared derived layer (recommended):* add `base_image` + `apt_packages` + `pip_packages` (+ a target-venv selector) + verbatim `run_commands` to `ResourceConfig`/`EnvironmentConfig`; Iris renders a Dockerfile, builds via the existing `DockerImageBuilder`/kaniko path, caches by content-hash(base + deps + commit), and pins the digest. Immutable, one-time cost, no per-run network. Needs a build service + registry-push creds.
2. *Setup-into-target-venv hook (lighter):* plumb `setup_scripts` + `--pip` / `--pip-venv <path>` through `remote()` and the CLI, and let `docker.py` activate a user-named venv instead of hardcoding `/app/.venv`. Zero build infra, but re-runs each job and gives no apt layer or immutable pin.

### Definition of Done

- Decide layer-build (1) vs. setup-hook (2).
- A user can add pip (and ideally apt) deps to a chosen base image + target venv from `ResourceConfig`/`remote()` without authoring a Dockerfile.
- The #7233 evalchemy case is expressible natively, or is documented as a legitimate custom-image case if it stays out of scope.

topics.title: SFT launcher: emit a chat-format TokenizedCache so num_train_steps can come from num_train_epochs
topics.body:
Follow-up to #7231 (general chat-SFT launcher).

`experiments/sft/configs/delphi_1e22.py` hand-computes `num_train_steps` as a packed 1-epoch count (`total_tokens / seq_len / weight / batch`), which is error-prone: `ChatLmDatasetFormat` packs several conversations per sequence, so a step count derived from raw row counts over-trains by that packing factor.

`marin.experiment.train.train_lm` already solves this with `num_train_epochs`: it reads `TokenizedCache.num_train_tokens` from a resolved dep at run time and computes `ceil(epochs * tokens / (seq_len * batch))`, which counts packed sequences correctly. The SFT launcher cannot reuse it today because:

1. Its deps are `transform_dataset_step` outputs (canonical OpenAI-messages documents), not tokenized caches — there is no `num_train_tokens` to read at build time; Levanter tokenizes/packs inside the training job via `auto_build_caches`.
2. `marin.experiment.data.tokenized` hardcodes `TextLmDatasetFormat` and cannot emit a chat cache (template + completions-only masking).

Proposal: add chat-format support to the marin tokenize helper so the SFT launcher can tokenize each source into a real chat `TokenizedCache` dep, then adopt the `train_lm` `num_train_epochs` path and drop the hand-computed `num_train_steps`.

topics.title: [grug] Source-push EP MoE follow-up (H100): review-ranked avenues on PR #6841 (SPF series)
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This follow-up to PR #6841 tests the best review-ranked ways to make source-push expert-parallel MoE competitive on EP8 H100s. The useful path is the staged semantic implementation: round 1 kept the bf16 `dy` cast, adopted XLA gather-sum combine, and confirmed host-side planning is the largest structural blocker, while owner-sharded `dx` return and fused W13 zero-fill fixes were falsified. The apparent W2-return regression was later traced to the deliberate W2-from-H boundary switch, not branch drift; SPF-008 recovered part of that cost by moving route scaling to the output side (w2_return 7.08 -> 6.36 ms), but naive double-buffering hurt occupancy. Current recommendation: continue on staged semantic/device-sided planning and occupancy-neutral W2-from-H overlap; keep the fused persistent-kernel path quarantined until it passes an integrated numerical gate.

### Helpful links
- PR #6841: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6841
- Round-1 results: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7276#issuecomment-4997344962
- SPF-007 root-cause note: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7276#issuecomment-4999175606
- SPF-008 result: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7276#issuecomment-5005358579
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Builds on #6597 / #6848 / PR #6841 at head `26711f86e`, target shape EP8 H100, 32768 tok/rank, top-k 4, 32 experts/rank, d2560/f1280, goal 250 useful TFLOP/s/rank fwd+bwd. Branch: `research/mcwitt/6841-source-push-followup`.

Ranked avenues (gain / effort):

1. `SPF-001` bf16-cast `dy` before the replicated reshard (`source_push_semantic_mlp.py:586`): all-gather payload 2.35 -> 1.17 GB, est. ~5.8 ms off the 63.0 ms API. S.
2. `SPF-002` switch dx return to the existing owner-sharded `psum_scatter` wrapper (`source_push_semantic_mlp.py:621`): all-reduce 4.70 -> 2.35 GB/rank, est. 3-6 ms. S.
3. `SPF-003a` measure unlogged tip commit `26711f86e` (grouped W13 raw gathers) vs the 23.025 ms fused-W13 baseline. Free.
4. `SPF-003b` fused W13-bwd unconditionally remote-writes a zero tile then overwrites it (`source_push_semantic_fused_w13_backward.py:1040`): 2x NVLink bytes on dX return, est. 2-4 ms of 135.5. S.
5. `SPF-004` combine kernel runs at ~21% of HBM roofline (per-row scalar loads, `source_push_combine.py:145`): 1.34 -> ~0.5 ms. S.
6. `SPF-005` host-side numpy planner cost at target shape is excluded from every benchmark number (O(268M) element ops/plan, `source_push_plan.py:636`): measure it. S, CPU-only.
7. Source-push dy route (fix dcombine in_specs `source_push_semantic_backward_pallas.py:2280`, reuse existing dy-route remote-write kernel + global phase barrier): rest of the 11.6 ms API tax. M-L.
8. W2-return kernel double-buffering + deferred `wait_smem_to_gmem` (`source_push_w2_return.py:680-765`): 4.05 -> ~2.7 ms. M.
9. Correctness cluster: single-jit remote-write completion barrier is scalar-only (`source_push_forward.py:1109`); fused dX-return has no wait on `ready_sem` before the combine kernel; integrated numerical gate FUSED-MOE-094 failed (y max-abs-diff 1024) and was never re-cleared. S-M, blocking for fused promotion.
10. SM-carveout restructure (persistent SM-capped comm kernels + pipelined near-stock GEMM consumers; de-fuse W2-return/combine as a dense fixed-shape permute): only credible route to 250. L, design first.

## Hypothesis or Goal

The S-effort tier (1+2+5) takes the honest API from 63.0 to ~50-52 ms (~150 useful) with grad parity, converging on the 44.2 ms manual bound; measurements 3/6 decide where the next M/L unit of work goes.

## Status

Round 1 complete (2026-07-16): SPF-001 keep (-1.87 ms, API 61.008 ms / 126.79 useful), SPF-002 falsified (VJP sharding contract), SPF-003a real but modest (-1.11%), SPF-003b falsified, SPF-004 adopt (XLA combine, bitwise-identical, 1745 GB/s) + W2 hoist keep, SPF-005 confirmed ~190x (380 ms/plan; ~1.85 s public path). New open items: SPF-006 compare-gate regression bisect. SPF-007 resolved from records (no bisect needed): the w2_return 4.05->7.08 ms jump is the deliberate W2-from-H boundary switch (`ae1c9aed1`+`e8fbfa85e`, 2026-07-03), measured contemporaneously; reclassified as avenue-8 kernel work. See round-1 comment and SPF-007 comment. SPF-008 (2026-07-17): avenue 8 executed on branch `spf/008-w2-from-h-kernel` — output-side route scaling ADOPTED (w2_return 7.077 -> 6.355 ms, total 16.72 -> 15.97; numerics bit-match the pre-change smoke; no new pytest failures vs head), 2-stage double-buffering FALSIFIED (8.57 ms: 2x SMEM halves CTA occupancy) and reverted; ~1.4 ms to the ~5.0 ms from_h floor remains, needs an occupancy-neutral overlap design. See SPF-008 comment. 2026-07-17: thread refocused on B200 (production priority) — continues in #7333 (SPB series); this issue is the H100 phase (retitled). Remaining H100 items (SPF-006 compare-gate bisect, occupancy-neutral W2-from-H overlap) deprioritized pending the SPB-001 gate.

* Prior logbooks: `.agents/logbooks/6597-moe-mgpu-forward.md`, `.agents/logbooks/6597-moe-fused-comm-tensorcore.md`
* Important updates:

## Decision Log

* 2026-07-17: refocus on B200 — production priority; B200 phase opened as #7333 (SPB series); this issue scoped to H100.
* 2026-07-16: perf spend goes to the staged semantic path; fused path gets free measurements + S-effort fixes only until it passes a finite integrated numerical gate.
* 2026-07-16: adopt XLA gather-sum combine (bitwise-identical, faster, deletes a kernel); keep bf16-dy cast and W2 weight-copy hoist; discard zero-fill fix and owner-sharded dx return.
* 2026-07-16: production viability of the public source-push API is gated on device-siding the planner (SPF-005) before any further kernel tuning; next perf unit of work is the SPF-007 bisect.
* 2026-07-17: SPF-008 — adopt output-side route scaling on the W2-from-H kernels (branch `spf/008-w2-from-h-kernel`, `aa38972c8`; -0.72 ms w2_return); reject naive double-buffering for these Lane kernels — overlap designs must keep SMEM under ~112 KB/CTA to preserve 2 CTAs/SM.
* 2026-07-16: SPF-007 closed without a bisect — root cause identified from the 6597 logbook records (W2-from-H switch is a priced-in H-boundary cost, head is +0.03 ms over the day-one 7.048 ms measurement); the recovery path is avenue 8 (output-side route scaling + double-buffered k-loop, ~4.5-5 ms target vs 6.80 ms post-hoist).

## Description

Publish the "Snowball" checkpoint — the Grug 67B-A2B intermediate cooldown trained on 2T tokens (of 10T) in #6811 — to Hugging Face so external users can try it. The hero run has landed and SFT/midtraining, chat templating, vLLM serving, and evals are green (announced 2026-07-17). Publishing was agreed in the #6811 thread: @hammer asked, @ClassicLarry and @yonromai concurred, with prerequisites noted below.

Final permanent checkpoint (Levanter/Grug format):
`gs://marin-us-central2/grug/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step39k-79ebf3/checkpoints/step-42150/`
(567 objects, ~539 GB; note step-**42150**, not 42149 — see https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6811#issuecomment-4952891213 correction by @yonromai). Regional mirrors already exist in `s3://marin-us-east-02a/...` and `gs://marin-us-east5/...`.

Prerequisites raised in the thread, which this task must resolve first:
- **Standardize the config against HF conventions** before export (@ClassicLarry).
- **Serialization contract for external use.** A Grug→safetensors export exists in `main` but was written for internal vLLM serving; it needs hardening for external consumers (@yonromai).

### Definition of Done

- Grug step-42150 checkpoint exported to safetensors with an HF-standard config, uploaded to a `marin-community` HF repo.
- Model card documents architecture (67B total / ~2B active MoE, d2560, 2T-token cooldown), provenance (links #6811), license, and the supported inference paths (Marin vLLM fork / Levanter), with a working load-and-generate snippet.
- Exported weights verified to produce outputs matching the source checkpoint under the Marin vLLM fork.

This is intentionally gated: @yonromai flagged in #6811 that we should not pay the upstreaming overhead "until the Grug architecture is more stable." File this to track the work and revisit once the arch settles.

topics.title: [evals] Run RULER long-context eval through the evalchemy fork
topics.body:
RULER (lm-eval's 13-task long-context group) synthesizes haystack prompts to exact token lengths, so it needs the served tokenizer and its `max_seq_lengths` ladder to reach lm-eval's TaskManager at data-prep time. Our evalchemy fork's `eval.eval` entrypoint builds the pretrain TaskManager without metadata and drops both `--metadata` and `--model_args`, so RULER crashes in `get_tokenizer` before generating anything. #7626 (being closed) worked around this by routing metadata-carrying tasks through lm-eval's own CLI (`python -m lm_eval`), which merges `model_args | metadata` into the TaskManager. That leaves two eval entrypoints in the marin client.

Decision on the #7626 thread (@Helw150, @penfever, @rjpower): keep evalchemy as the single source of truth for our evals and fix the fork so RULER runs through `eval.eval` consistently, rather than carrying a direct lm-eval CLI path in the marin client.

Evalchemy-side work (fork `marin-community/evalchemy`, pinned in `docker/evalchemy-tpu/Dockerfile` at `EVALCHEMY_COMMIT=e006f2e9e0df606179f397e77ae1883b47d2e80b`):

- Teach `eval.eval` to merge `--metadata` and `--model_args` into the TaskManager it builds, the way lm-eval's own CLI does (`lm_eval/config/evaluate_config.py::_process_arguments` merges `model_args | metadata`, then `process_tasks(cfg.metadata)` builds the TaskManager from that). Today the fork constructs the pretrain TaskManager without metadata, so `simple_evaluate`'s `metadata` argument never applies and both flags are silently dropped for lm-eval-native tasks. This is the core change: it surfaces the served tokenizer and the `max_seq_lengths` ladder into RULER's `custom_dataset`.
- Bake lm-eval's `[ruler]` runtime deps into the evalchemy-tpu image (`wonderwords`, `scipy`; `nltk` is already baked), rebuild `:evalchemy-tpu-<gitsha>`, live-TPU smoke it, promote the floating tag, and re-pin the image digest in `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runtime.py` (`EVALCHEMY_IMAGE`). #7626 already stages these deps in the Dockerfile; this step is the rebuild + digest re-pin, alongside bumping `EVALCHEMY_COMMIT` to the fork commit carrying the metadata fix.

Marin-side follow-up, once the fork forwards metadata:

- Collapse the routing shim in `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/client.py`: the `native = bool(task.get("metadata"))` branch that routes to `python -m lm_eval` returns to the single `eval.eval` path. The served-window clamp (`fit_context_lengths`) and the `EvalTaskConfig.metadata` plumbing stay. #7626 carries the launcher definitions (`ruler`, `ruler-smoke`, and a `longcontext` suite), the clamp, and the tests to port.

Reimplements the stale WIP #6110. Parent: #6503.

Done when: a `ruler` launch runs end-to-end through `eval.eval` against a served endpoint with no direct `python -m lm_eval` path in the marin client, RULER scores land under the standard results layout, and the evalchemy-tpu image ships the `[ruler]` deps with its digest pinned.

topics.title: [eval] Resume existing Harbor runs for selective recovery
topics.body:
Resume an existing Harbor evaluation with `--resume-run-id`, then optionally retry its unscored trials with `--retry-unscored-harbor-trials`. The launcher reads the saved record and reuses the original run ID and results directory instead of creating an empty output tree.

Recovery requires one Harbor evaluation with the original model, hosted judge, policy, runtime, and version. The current error taxonomy preserves scored outcomes, including zero-reward agent failures, and leaves unknown errors available for diagnosis. A launcher regression covers persisted results, selective recovery, and rejection of a changed checkpoint under the same model name.

Resume only after the original Iris group and any earlier retry have ended. A saved record can be stale while a retry is running, so the launcher cannot detect concurrent drivers from the record alone. Missing-record errors identify the selected prefix and point to the platform, accelerator, and records-prefix controls.

Fixes #9100

topics.title: [experiment] Hero 535B at 65K on H100: 15.5% MFU with PP24/EP8
topics.body:
## TL;DR

The full 535B, 48-layer Hero model completed ten finite synthetic updates at sequence length 65,536 on 192 H100s with **15.523% median MFU and 174.432 seconds per step**. The working recipe is standard 1F1B, PP24/EP8, batch 384 (48 pipeline microbatches), BF16 MuonH, and host activation/optimizer offload. Keep batch 384 as the best measured throughput recipe; CP2 provides the validated batch 96 alternative. Stop DualPipeV performance exploration for now. DualPipeV also completed ten updates, but required extra recomputation, cotangent offload, and task waits and reached only 4.917% MFU.

CP2 also completed ten full-model updates with finite losses at **batch 96 (6Mi tokens), 9.877% MFU and 68.539 seconds/update**, with all 24 workers exiting successfully. This uses PP24/EP4/CP2: each GPU handles 32K tokens of each 65K sequence. The earlier 15.523% result uses batch 384 (24Mi tokens), so these are different throughput/batch tradeoffs.

Here Mi means 2^20 tokens. These are bounded systems diagnostics from fresh initialization with synthetic data. Production checkpoint continuation, long-run stability, and training quality remain unvalidated. No production GB200 run was changed.

## Description

Adapted `experiments/grug/moe_pipeline/pipeline.py` to Hero's actual blocks, preserving the model shape, latent/shared experts, SConv, absolute local/global attention schedule, and QB router updates. The full model has 535,477,106,688 parameters, 48 layers, width 6144, 384 routed experts, top-8 routing, and latent/expert intermediate width 3072. FA4 (`gpu_fa4_cute`) is active. No FP8 was needed.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Establish a memory-safe H100 recipe for the existing Hero shape at 32K and 65K, then improve utilization by filling the pipeline without changing the core model.

## Status

### Validated 65K 1F1B scaling

All rows use the full model, 192 H100s on `cw-rno2a`, PP24/EP8, one process per eight-GPU node, six expert transport waves, BF16 MuonH, both host offloads, and explicit device completion after each update. Every row completed ten finite updates with all 24 workers exiting successfully.

| Microbatches | Global batch | Median seconds/step | Median MFU | Run |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 8 | 64 | 64.626 | 6.983% | [m8](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-1f1b-ep8-65k-full-m8-sync-20260918-19) |
| 16 | 128 | 86.743 | 10.405% | [m16](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-1f1b-ep8-65k-full-m16-sync-20260918-21) |
| 24 | 192 | 108.584 | 12.468% | [m24](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-1f1b-ep8-65k-full-m24-sync-20260918-22) |
| 32 | 256 | 130.207 | 13.864% | [m32](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-1f1b-ep8-65k-full-m32-sync-20260918-23) |
| 48 | 384 | 174.432 | 15.523% | [m48](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-1f1b-ep8-65k-full-m48-sync-20260918-24) |

The maximum standard-1F1B activation backlog caps at 24 microbatches. Increasing batch beyond m24 improved pipeline occupancy without increasing that maximum backlog. The m48 final loss was 11.62364388. The reported step timer excludes some global loss collection/inter-step overhead; these comparisons use the same timer and model FLOP accounting.

Earlier full-model milestones: 32K completed three updates at batch 8 (~18.84 seconds, ~1.28% MFU); 65K batch 8 completed ten (~65.69 seconds, ~0.859%). Short-context DualPipeV reached ~13.91% median MFU with AdamW and ~13.72% with MuonH; those are different batch/context recipes and do not establish long-context superiority.

### H100 context parallelism: smaller global batch

[Full CP2 run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-cp2-full-65k-20260919-06) preserved the 535B/48-layer model and 65,536-token sequences on the same 192 H100s. It used PP24/EP4/CP2, 24 pipeline microbatches, global batch 96, BF16 MuonH, six expert waves, both host offloads, and the existing per-update device-completion workaround. Ten losses were finite (11.792197 → 11.449181); all 24 Iris and native exits were zero.

| Configuration | Pipeline microbatches | Global batch | Tokens/update | Median seconds/update | Median MFU |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| PP24/EP8/CP1 | 24 | 192 | 12Mi | 108.584 | 12.468% |
| PP24/EP4/CP2 | 24 | 96 | 6Mi | 68.539 | 9.877% |
| PP24/EP8/CP1, best throughput | 48 | 384 | 24Mi | 174.432 | 15.523% |

CP2 halves sequence length per GPU to 32K and global microbatch from eight sequences to four. With the same PP24 topology and 24 pipeline microbatches, it halves tokens/update; reducing microbatch count from the previous best's 48 to 24 reduces total batch by another factor of two. CP2 processes fewer tokens per update and has a shorter measured update time, at lower token throughput. The step timer excludes some global loss collection/inter-step overhead. The runs also use different FlashAttention/CuTe helper versions, so this is not an isolated CP-only speed comparison.

Validation before the full run:

- Three two-H100 CP2-versus-CP1 BF16 attention cases passed: causal, sliding window 2048, and packed/padded sequences. Outputs matched exactly; maximum absolute dQ error was 0.0004883 and dK/dV error was 0.03125 with absolute and relative tolerances both 0.07. Native SM90 support is in #9282, based on #9117.
- A five-layer, width-8, six-token CPU model matched CP2 pipeline versus CP1 unsplit-model loss and all parameter gradients with absolute and relative tolerances both 1e-5, including packed boundaries, SConv and activation offload. The next-token label shift requires gathering token IDs across CP before shifting; hidden activations remain sequence-sharded.
- Two full-width blocks at 65K passed repeated gradient and host-state MuonH updates on eight H100s. An eight-layer PP4/EP4/CP2 pipeline then passed ten updates on 32 H100s.
- The pipeline environment initially selected FA4 b16, which lacks `AuxData`. The validated CP stack uses FA4 b28, CUTLASS DSL 4.6.2 and Quack 0.6.4 while retaining JAX/JAXlib 0.11.0 for JAXPP.

CP2 launch source: `c55ab40a29c4bda8d1ed54c7e31ddbbbff209e8f`, combining the open CP stack through #9119, #9282, and the Hero pipeline adapter. The full run used the same scratch JAXPP/Dime2 overlays as the successful smaller gate, plus the explicit helper versions above. The launcher applied the helper versions above during setup; the equivalent dependency declarations were subsequently recorded locally in `3ad8d3ce37ded02c956d9811865119f8f189c71e`; the five-file CP integration and dependency update are published in draft #9283 above a dependency-only base combining #9119, #9282 and #9279. The draft still requires the scratch runtime fixes described below. Evidence: `cp2-full-65k06-evidence.json`, `cp2-pp4-65k05-evidence.json`, `cp-fullwidth65k-muon04-evidence.json` and `cp-sm90-parity02-evidence.json` under `scratch/hero-h100-20260916/`.

### Memory and correctness findings

- JAXPP mesh rebinding failed to preserve Host/Device memory targets: minimal reproduction in [NVIDIA/jaxpp#13](https://github.com/NVIDIA/jaxpp/issues/13).
- Forward partitioning moved activation D2H copies into backward. Keeping copies in forward and preserving pinned-host intermediate shardings saved exactly **12 GiB/device** at eight outstanding microbatches in the 24-layer diagnostic (first-backward live memory 26.10 → 14.10 GiB). CPU actual-partition value/gradient tests and GPU host ABI checks passed.
- Embedding recomputation reduced stage-zero activation retention. Parking real state on host during disposable warmup avoids holding real and warmup model copies on GPU together.
- The working allocator settings are `cuda_async`, memory fraction 0.91, preallocation false. BFC trials encountered large-allocation failures despite aggregate free space. Raising preallocation to 0.95 also caused an NCCL allocation failure.
- Two unsynchronized full m8 runs produced NaNs at updates 10 and 8. Finite-state instrumentation passed, and explicit completion of all eight local GPUs after each update passed repeatedly. This supports a timing association; **the race/root cause is unresolved**. Small fixed-weight host-lifetime and receive-buffer-reuse probes passed and did not reproduce the failure.
- The Dime2 send-capsule lifetime fix is already available in [upstream 78458f8](https://github.com/NVIDIA/jaxpp/commit/78458f8b258f0fd467be13b4b8e7056a853e320b). The diagnostic stack backports it; this is not a new upstream contribution.

### DualPipeV negative results

Full topology: 48 logical / 24 physical stages, EP8, 48 microbatches, batch 384, same 65K context and model.

- Splitting activation and weight backward generated ~13.24 GiB of retained device intermediates per delayed weight backward. Independent recomputation removed those residuals but added compute.
- Offloading original delayed cotangents removed another memory constraint. Full warmup then passed, but asynchronous real execution OOM'd in `bwdA_40` on the first update. Free-memory counters printed after failure do not prove fragmentation.
- Waiting for each task's outputs completed ten updates: [full35](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-dualpipe-ep8-65k-full-taskwait-20260919-35), 565.108 seconds, 4.791% MFU.
- Waiting only around backward tasks also completed ten, all 24 native exits zero: [full37](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-dualpipe-ep8-65k-full-bwdwait-20260919-37), 550.704 seconds, 4.917% MFU, final loss 11.62360668. Only ~2.5% faster. Diagnostic memory logging remained enabled; its overhead and recomputation/transfer costs were not separately measured.
- Eight expert waves regressed the eight-layer diagnostic: 55.17 vs 46.52 seconds, recorded peak 68.97 vs 67.27 GiB. Rejected.

## Links

- Related GB200 EP investigation: #7279.
- Runtime incident record: https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/445
- Original CP1 source base: `96da2a6cdce401187239846957687fdde22cf8a5`; JAXPP pin used for overlays: `46b8443eed01f54688dd24ae451203a504b1cff8`.
- Local evidence/manifests: `scratch/hero-h100-20260916/`, especially `full65k-m48-sync24-evidence.json`, `dual65k-full-taskwait35-evidence.json`, and `dual65k-full-bwdwait37-evidence.json`. These ignored workspace artifacts are not a published reproduction package. W&B links above retain the run evidence.

## Decision Log

- Preserve core Hero shape; use BF16 and MuonH with both offloads; no FP8 required.
- Keep 1F1B at 65K/batch384 as the working result. End further DualPipeV throughput sweeps and prepare reviewable changes.
- Build on the existing open CP stack (#9116–#9119), as authorized; port its native attention backward to SM90. CP2 now validates the full model at batch96/6Mi tokens. No competing CP implementation was introduced.

## Conclusion

15.523% MFU establishes bounded full-model 65K feasibility on H100s at batch384/24Mi tokens. CP2 establishes a smaller batch96/6Mi alternative at 9.877% MFU. Prepare separate changes for (1) the small Muon expert-stack sharding fix and regression, (2) upstream JAXPP memory-space and forward-host-residual correctness fixes, and (3) the Hero pipeline adapter, runner, tests, and documented recipe. Treat startup warmup APIs as a separate dependency and keep DualPipeV-only overlays/telemetry out of the minimal 1F1B stack. A clean dependency pin and reproducible launcher still need to replace the scratch overlays before claiming stock-install reproduction. Retain the step-completion workaround until its underlying timing issue is understood.

topics.title: Clear masked shared-memory tiles in segmented FA4 backward
topics.body:
Clear masked shared-memory entries before the existing segmented FA4 backward kernel copies queries, keys, values, and output gradients. Its synchronous copies leave masked destinations unchanged, but matrix operations still read those entries. Stale NaNs can therefore propagate through products with zero.

Add a GB200 test that repeatedly compares partial-tile outputs and gradients against the float32 reference.

Extracted from #9228. This fixes the existing segmented kernel independently of native SM100 kernel selection.

The [GB200 regression](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fmwittmann%2Ffa4-scope-port-20260922b) passes. The run used CPU Torch 2.11.0 to avoid main’s unrelated `libcufile.so.0` import failure. Seven affected safe tests pass locally; lint and type checks pass.

topics.title: Add correctness-gated GDN-2 TPU kernels
topics.body:
Add experimental single-device Gated DeltaNet-2 kernels and a correctness-gated benchmark. Vendor only Atomic Ops' four compute files at a9bd7c5315907d23ccf1ce6b033d46a196566888 as the baseline, retaining the MIT license and original arithmetic. The modified candidate replaces off-diagonal pairwise exponentiation and reduction with matrix products, and masks noncausal pairs before exponentiation. It has no clipping, non-finite replacement, or solve damping.

Repeated matched sweeps show 3.05–3.27x faster forward+backward on v5e/v5p and 3.12–3.22x on v6e than each device's fastest tested baseline configuration, for batches 4/8, 4096 tokens, and six 128-dimensional heads in FP32/BF16. The v6e forward-only speedup is 5.36–5.62x. Outputs, final state, and gradients for q/k/v/w/b/g and the initial state pass an independent CPU recurrence before either timing mode is accepted. All four TPU generations select 128-token chunks; the solve microblock is 16 tokens on v4/v5e/v5p and 32 on v6e. Batches 5–7 are unmeasured interpolation.

The v4 candidate passes the same representative shapes; all four hardware types pass separate batch-1, 512-token stress tests with log-decays sampled down to -5. The baseline does not compile on v4; no baseline speedup is claimed there. The v4 256-token configuration exceeds VMEM. Its selected 128-token, batch-8 FP32 forward-only measurements include periodic outliers. v6e's selected tile repeats within 0.22%, but other tile configurations also show outliers. All timing samples are retained.

[Measurement artifacts](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3df6efef5a0fb18928e72673e9fd5f769749ae15/docs/reports/data/gdn2-tpu-20260922/README.md) retain exact source snapshots, hardware settings, compilation costs, and caveats. The [kernel reference](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3df6efef5a0fb18928e72673e9fd5f769749ae15/docs/references/gdn2-kernels.md) documents reproduction and explicit tuning fallback. Affected unit tests, lint/type checks, and documentation-link checks pass. Model integration and training are outside this change.

topics.title: [vllm histograms] Store and query cumulative family snapshots
topics.body:
Store cumulative histograms as one record per engine and family. The opt-in Rigging publisher preserves collected integer bins, bounds, and collection metadata using existing `kind=histogram` records and nullable `body_json`. Raw histogram observations and the scalar publisher retain their behavior. No new record kind, table, column, backfill, or database/schema migration is required.

The detailed and compact dashboard readers share publication validation and interval-delta logic for scalar, structured, and mixed histories, including output length and time per output token. Equivalent numeric bounds share schema identity for interval baselines. Duplicate checks retain the original encoded bounds, so differing copies of one identified publication are excluded by both views. Dual writes are matched by publication identity. Counts support 0 through 2^63−1; unsupported source counts are reported as loss. Scalar counts at or above 2^53 are unavailable for exact deltas, and multiple bucket schemas withhold percentile/distribution estimates. The root DuckDB lock matches Grafana's 1.5.4.

The [design and local measurement report](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/773) documents the wire contract, ownership, and September 23–24, 2026 results: 6,208→832 data rows, 8→2 HTTP POSTs, 83.0% fewer compressed request bytes, and 180.17→33.50 seconds ingest in a four-engine, three-hour replay. Detailed client peak RSS was higher (441→474 MB). These historical measurements do not prove current-head performance, training speed, or #9382's seven-day/50-job ten-second target.

The companion producer is marin-community/MarinSkyRL#738. Activation requires the released Rigging API, frozen structured/dual delivery checks, regional-schema and external-consumer verification, server/reader deployment, and a bounded training canary. Part of #9382.

topics.title: [grug] Register symmetric buffers for hero all-gather and reduce-scatter
topics.body:
On the ragged all-to-all backend, the hero template registers NCCL symmetric buffers for the model's all-gather and reduce-scatter collectives in addition to the ragged transport. Levanter's `RAGGED_REQUIRED_XLA_FLAGS` keeps only the `raggedalltoall` registration that the device-initiated transport needs, so other users of that constant, such as the ragged EP test harness, are unchanged. The template keeps the flag non-overridable, like the transport flags.

Against #9333 alone, this change makes a typical update 0.24% faster, but it does not yet show a significant gain in mean throughput. Each arm ran twice on the same rack of 64 GB200 GPUs, in the order #9333, this PR, this PR, #9333. The trees were #9333 at `f56f7e6a9e` and this PR at `2698045acf`, which differ only in this change. The #9333 tree has the same dependency locks, hero model, training, and kernel code as `main` after #9333 merged. Each run restored the permanent hero `2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-30000` checkpoint with the production data mixture, batch 1024, sequence length 4096, and one process per GPU. Each run discarded 20 warmup updates and scored the 40 updates from 30020 through 30059. Every run sees the same batch at each step, so steps are compared across arms by step number.

| Configuration | Mean step time | Median step time | Mean iteration time | MFU | Runs |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| #9333 | 13.917 s | 13.906 s | 14.146 s | 28.21% | [a](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-symab2-base-a-20260923), [b](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-symab2-base-b-20260923) |
| This PR | 13.905 s | 13.882 s | 14.128 s | 28.23% | [a](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-symab2-sym-a-20260923), [b](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-symab2-sym-b-20260923) |

This PR was faster on 34 of 40 matched steps (sign test p = 8e-6). Two updates in run a took 14.96 s and 14.40 s. Excluding those steps, it saves 33 ms per update (standard error 6 ms), or 0.24%. Including them, mean training throughput improves by 0.09% (95% bootstrap interval −0.17% to +0.27%), and iteration throughput by 0.13%. None of the #9333 runs had an update slower than 14.18 s. In an earlier campaign on the same rack, updates slower than 14.3 s occurred in all three arms, including the #9366 control, so these runs do not show whether symmetric buffers cause them. Losses stayed finite. The largest matched-step loss difference was 0.00051, the same as between the two #9333 runs. An earlier three-run campaign, on the same rack and an earlier revision of #9333, measured a 0.32% mean gain ([a](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-maskab-both-a-20260922), [b](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-maskab-both-b-20260922), [c](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-maskab-both-c-20260922)).

Without the mask removal, symmetric buffers had no mean benefit: on PR #9228 revision `b688829e3d`, they measured −0.03% against the control ([a](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-opt-fa4-symmetric-a-20260922), [b](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-opt-fa4-symmetric-b-20260922), [c](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-opt-fa4-symmetric-c-20260922)), and slow updates in two repetitions erased an improvement in the median. A full [d768 run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ep-opt-d768-replayed-treatment-20260922) of 11,420 updates with both changes completed 20 dropless evaluations and matched the [historical control](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/validate9215-d768-20260917) to +0.000105 nats mean training loss.

Two risks remain untested at hero scale. The hero's parameters shard only within a rack, so each all-gather and reduce-scatter buffer should be the same size at 1 and 11 racks; whether XLA lowers any cross-rack gradient reduction as a symmetric-registered reduce-scatter or all-gather has not been checked. The dropless evaluator now also registers a symmetric window. #8861 showed that XLA resolves an address to the last window registered at the collective-memory arena base, so a smaller eval window can shadow the train step's; the d768 run passed its evaluations, but the hero shape has not been tested with interleaved evaluation.

Draft until those checks run.

topics.title: [grug] Close FA4 SM100 review follow-ups
topics.body:
Close the open review items from #9332.

The native SM100 FA4 dispatch now rejects unsupported layouts in both directions. Before, with `sm100_backward` set, the backward quietly fell back to the port kernel for shapes outside BF16, D128 and GQA ratios 4, 6 and 8, using the placeholder port fields of the SM100 config. One `validate_sm100_layout` check now defines the supported shapes for the entry point, forward and backward.

`gpu_fa4_cute_sm100` and the native tile sweep accept every compute capability 10.x, matching upstream FA4, which runs its SM100 kernels on all of them, and the removed `gpu_fa4_cute_wide` backend. SM103 (GB300/B300) has not been validated on hardware.

The native SM90 backward now passes the context-parallel query offset to its kernel mask; it previously passed zero while its sparse metadata used the real offset. The frontend no longer swaps H100 sequence-sharded attention onto the 64×64 segmented backward.

Left out: hoisting the per-layer sparse-metadata rebuild out of the layer scan. At the hero's per-device shape (B=16, S=4096), a forward-plus-backward metadata build takes about 0.3 ms on CPU. The hero does about 144 builds per step, which comes to roughly 5 ms, or 0.03% of a ~15 s step on 64 GB200s. Sequence sharding would also need per-shard precompute, because the backward block lists cannot be sliced from one global build.

GPU validation is pending: the SM90 context-parallel path needs the sequence-sharded parity test on H100, and the SM100 paths need the FA4 GPU tests on GB200.

topics.title: Marin Eval Policy (2026-09-24)
topics.body:
## Overview

What is this document? This document is an attempt to formalize Marin’s policy towards what constitutes reportable, public-facing, canonical eval results for Marin models as well as the baselines we compare against.

Why do we need this document? With the first “snowball” release of a 67B A2B MoE, Marin is entering a regime where we regularly compare Marin models to existing open and closed-source models. Because Marin’s unique claim is that we are open development, we will need to hold ourselves to a high standard of transparency on how we report eval scores of Marin models and what claims we make about Marin model capabilities based on those scores.

What is in scope for this document? This document is intended to act as a living snapshot, trustworthy for any given period in time, as to the what and the how of Marin’s canonical set of evals, a set of standards to which we will aspire to hold ourselves. By "the what", we mean “which evals did we run, with what consistent set of hyperparameters and experimental constraints”. By "the how", we mean “where is the self-contained codebase that is both necessary and sufficient to reproduce our eval results independently”.

### Details on our Evals

- **MATH-500.** OpenAI's [May 2023 process-supervision release](https://openai.com/index/improving-mathematical-reasoning-with-process-supervision/) used a 500-problem subset of the original MATH competition-math benchmark. The campaign scores one zero-shot generated solution per problem by final-answer accuracy.
- **HumanEval+.** The [May 2023 EvalPlus paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01210) introduced expanded tests for HumanEval programs to catch incorrect code that passes sparse original tests. The campaign executes one zero-shot completion per problem against the stronger tests.
- **MBPP+.** The [November 24, 2023 EvalPlus release](https://github.com/evalplus/evalplus/releases/tag/v0.2.0) extends MBPP with additional functional tests. The campaign's pinned config is zero-shot and scores one generated program per problem.
- **OlympiadBench.** The [February 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14008) introduced bilingual, multimodal Olympiad-level math and science problems. This campaign uses Evalchemy's 30-question text subset, ten sampled solutions per question, and the configured answer judge.
- **GSM8K.** The [October 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168) introduced grade-school math word problems requiring multi-step arithmetic. The campaign uses the zero-shot `gsm8k-0shot` completion route and scores the extracted final answer.
- **PIQA.** The [November 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.11641) introduced two-choice questions about physical commonsense. The campaign selects the answer by length-normalized log-likelihood with no examples in the prompt.
- **WinoGrande.** The [July 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10641) introduced adversarial pronoun/coreference choices designed to reduce superficial cues. The campaign uses five-shot multiple-choice scoring.
- **BoolQ.** The [May 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10044) introduced naturally occurring yes/no questions paired with evidence passages. The campaign scores zero-shot choice accuracy.
- **TruthfulQA MC2.** The [September 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.07958) introduced questions that elicit common misconceptions from language models. The campaign's MC2 metric sums probability mass on all true answers within each question's candidate set, rather than counting a single selected answer.
- **TriviaQA.** The [May 2017 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.03551) introduced trivia questions with independently collected evidence documents. The campaign runs five-shot answer generation and reports answer accuracy.
- **AIME24.** The [Mathematical Association of America's 2024 AIME](https://maa.org/maa-invitational-competitions/) supplies the contest problems; AIME24 is a year-specific evaluation set, not a separately introduced research benchmark. Evalchemy samples ten solutions per question through the benchmark's built-in repeat loop and scores the integer final answers. The campaign ran that 30-question, ten-repeat protocol ten times, for 3,000 generations per model. The preserved launch records have `evalchemy.seed: null`, so the outer launches were not ten distinct random seeds; every launch used the same benchmark-internal repeat seed schedule.
- **MMLU-Pro.** The [June 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01574) introduced harder, more reasoning-focused multiple-choice questions across fourteen subjects. The campaign runs zero-shot generation with a 65,536-token cap and reports micro-averaged accuracy.
- **GPQA Diamond.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12022) introduced expert-written graduate-level science questions, including the Diamond subset. The campaign averages accuracy over three generated answers per question.
- **CRUXEval (output).** The [January 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03065) introduced input- and output-prediction tasks for short Python programs. The tracker reports the output-prediction direction, scored on one generated answer per item.
- **FinanceBench.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11944) introduced questions grounded in public financial filings. The campaign scores one generated answer per question with its pinned LLM judge.
- **IFBench.** The [July 2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02833) introduced verifiable constraints that test generalization in precise instruction following. The campaign reports strict prompt-level accuracy, requiring every constraint to hold in the raw response.
- **MRCR.** [Gemini's September 2024 report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640) introduced multi-round coreference resolution; [OpenAI's public MRCR release (April 2025)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr) supplies the corrected multi-needle data used here. The campaign scores nonce-gated sequence similarity and selects only context-length bins that fit the served model.
- **NUPA.** The [November 2024 Number Cookbook paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03766) introduced tests of numerical understanding and processing across representations and tasks. Existing tracker scores use the full Evalchemy protocol of 238,926 selected prompts.
- **SWE-bench Verified random-100.** OpenAI's [August 13, 2024 release](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/) introduced a human-validated subset of repository-issue repair tasks. The campaign evaluates a fixed random 100-task subset of this existing subset, with one Terminus-2 trial per issue and executable verification.
- **OpenThoughts-TBLite 2.0.** The [February 18, 2026 release](https://www.openthoughts.ai/blog/openthoughts-tblite) introduced a 100-task, faster-running terminal-agent panel calibrated against Terminal-Bench 2. The campaign runs its pinned `openthoughts-tblite@2.0` tasks with Terminus-2 and reports verifier success.
- **Terminal-Bench 2.0.** The [November 7, 2025 release](https://www.tbench.ai/news/announcement-2-0) introduced a harder, more thoroughly verified terminal-agent task set alongside Harbor. The campaign uses the pinned TB2 dataset through Harbor with one Terminus-2 trial per task.
- **DS-1000 mini-200.** The [November 2022 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11501) introduced data-science code-generation problems spanning seven Python libraries. The campaign evaluates a fixed seed-42 200-task Harbor subset with Terminus-2, building task images from the pinned Dockerfiles.
- **BFCL-Parity @ Pi.** Berkeley's [February 2024 BFCL release](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/blogs/8_berkeley_function_calling_leaderboard.html) introduced executable function-calling evaluation. This campaign uses the Harbor `bfcl_parity@1.0` adaptation with the Pi agent, so its score is the pinned adaptation's verified solve rate rather than an unqualified BFCL leaderboard score.
- **BixBench CLI corrections @ Pi.** The [February 2025 BixBench paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00096) introduced multi-step computational-biology analysis tasks. This campaign uses Pi on 205 `bixbench-cli-marin-corrections@3` tasks and reports binary answer-equivalence reward, which is distinct from canonical BixBench CLI v1.5.
- **τ³-bench @ Pi.** Sierra's [March 18, 2026 τ³-Bench launch](https://sierra.ai/blog/bench-advancing-agent-benchmarking-to-knowledge-and-voice) introduced knowledge and voice tracks alongside corrections to the existing airline and retail tasks. The campaign runs pinned `tau3-bench@1.0.1` in Harbor through the Pi ACP relay and scores task verification.
- **SOTOPIA-hard.** The [October 2023 SOTOPIA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11667) introduced interactive social-agent evaluation and identified a hard scenario subset. The campaign runs the 100 hard episodes against a fixed `openai/gpt-oss-120b` counterpart and judge, then normalizes goal achievement from 0–10 to 0–1.

### How do we handle in-distribution and out-of-distribution evals?

#### IN-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- dedup against our SFT data, look at model scores while we develop the model, inspect the correlation of our ID evals with our OOD evals

**We may** -- develop synthetic RL tasks modeled on specific tasks in ID evals

**We will not** -- train on teacher rollouts from eval questions, use our ID eval instructions directly as the basis of RL data

#### OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- de-dup against our SFT raw data, look at meta-data about these evals (e.g., how big they are, general knowledge domain, etc), eval baselines on these evals

**We may** -- evaluate our final models on out-of-distribution benchmarks

**We will not** -- look at the individual questions in the evals, look at any of our own model scores from these evals until our model is frozen, model any synthetic tasks on tasks in the evals (edited)

### Metric definitions

- **`accuracy`:** the fraction of scored items that pass the benchmark's configured correctness check. The common name covers executable-test success for code and agent tasks, answer correctness for generated and multiple-choice tasks, FinanceBench's `correct` judge label, and BixBench's binary answer-equivalence check. NUPA counts an item as correct only when its format-specific extraction produces a representation-sensitive exact match. PIQA chooses the option with the highest length-normalized log-likelihood before testing correctness. AIME24 first averages its ten built-in repeats per question and then averages across ten outer launches; the outer launches did not pass distinct seeds. GPQA-Diamond and OlympiadBench average their three and ten in-run repeats per question. MMLU-Pro is micro-averaged across its fourteen subjects.
- **`mc2`:** TruthfulQA's probability mass on all true answers, normalized over the question's answer set and averaged over questions. It is not a binary selection accuracy, and chance performance is above zero.
- **`accuracy (output)`:** CRUXEval output-prediction accuracy. Given a function and input, the model predicts the output; this is distinct from CRUXEval input prediction, which reconstructs an input from the function and desired output.
- **`strict prompt-level accuracy`:** the fraction of IFBench prompts for which the raw response satisfies every required constraint.
- **`mean sequence similarity`:** MRCR's mean `SequenceMatcher` ratio between the response's answer span and the reference answer. A response that fails MRCR's nonce check receives zero credit. The standard 73,728-token serving window evaluates the published bins through 65,536 tokens. After Marin's 64-token serving safety margin, the 32,768-token models use bins through 16,384 and the 65,536-token model uses bins through 32,768. Those tracker cells are footnoted because differing bin coverage is not a strictly like-for-like comparison.
- **`normalized goal achievement`:** SOTOPIA-hard's official goal-achievement score for the evaluated character, linearly normalized from `[0, 10]` to `[0, 1]` and averaged over the 100 official hard episodes. The counterpart and evaluator are fixed to `openai/gpt-oss-120b` on Together for every model.

### Other Metric Notes

- **Scale:** every metric in the suite is reported on a 0-1 scale with 1 the best and 0 the worst; there are no error counts, ranks, or unbounded scores.
- **Allowed context length:** This is allowed prompt + completion context length. If a model's maximum context length is less than the allowed context length, we adopt the model's maximum context length. For single-turn benchmarks, we subdivide the space into max prompt length = longest prompt in the dataset plus a bit of cushion, max response length = the remaining context window. For standard multi-turn benchmarks, max generation length per turn is capped at 8192. Context-ablation labels are `context window / per-turn output limit`: both values are passed explicitly, with the first applied to vLLM `max_model_len` and Pi `model_info.max_input_tokens`, and the second applied to Pi `model_info.max_output_tokens`. For example, `65k-16k` means a 65,536-token serving and Pi context window with a 16,384-token per-turn output limit.
- **Pi runtime:** Agentic Pi configs must pin `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` explicitly. The corrected context control pins Pi `0.87.0`; the original harness result used unpinned Pi `0.86.1`, while the first context-ablation rerun drifted to unpinned Pi `0.87.0`. Results from different Pi versions are not treated as a controlled context-only comparison.

### LLM judges

Four evals involve an LLM judge; every other eval in the suite grades programmatically
(IFBench verifies each constraint with its checker functions, MRCR uses `SequenceMatcher`,
the math evals use Minerva/SymPy, the multiple-choice evals compare selections, and the
harness/agentic evals run test suites).

- **FinanceBench:** every scored response is judged. The judge sees the question, the
  reference answers, and the candidate, and returns one label: `correct`, `incorrect`, or
  `not_attempted` (equivalent answers in substance count as correct — algebraic equivalence,
  unit conversions, rounding). Only `correct` scores.
- **BixBench CLI correction set:** every submitted answer is judged for semantic equivalence
  to the task's ideal answer and receives a binary reward. A missing answer receives zero
  without invoking the judge.
- **OlympiadBench:** Minerva/SymPy grades first, and the judge answers equivalence only for
  answers Minerva cannot establish; the reported scores come from the offline regrade, which
  uses this judge the same way (see "OlympiadBench regrade" below).
- **SOTOPIA-hard:** the official episode evaluator judges goal achievement for the evaluated
  character after each completed social interaction and returns the 0–10 score that the metric
  normalizes to 0–1.

The standard judge for all four is `openai/gpt-oss-120b` served through Together
(`JUDGE_MODEL`/`JUDGE_BASE_URL` in the launch commands; the credential is the Together API
key). Open weights and one model everywhere keep judge behavior consistent across evals and
runs, and reproducible anywhere Together (or a self-serve vLLM deployment of the same
checkpoint) is available. τ³'s LiteLLM client uses `openai/openai/gpt-oss-120b`: the first
segment selects LiteLLM's OpenAI-compatible provider and the remainder is Together's model ID.
Judge hyperparameters, per path:

- **Answer-equivalence judge** (FinanceBench, OlympiadBench): a single user message with the
  three-way rubric, `temperature=0`, request timeout 300 s with 5 transport retries, and 16
  concurrent judgments per run. `max_tokens` starts at 128 and escalates 128 → 512 → 2048
  when a completion comes back empty — a hosted reasoning model can spend a small completion
  budget on hidden reasoning and return no content — so the ladder guarantees the final label
  lands within budget. The context window is gpt-oss-120b's 131,072 tokens as served
  (Together); no truncation of the graded material happens judge-side. The raw completion is
  retained in the results for audit, alongside the parsed label.
- **BixBench verifier:** the verifier calls Chat Completions with `max_tokens=1024` and a
  structured response schema containing one boolean score. Sampling follows the endpoint's
  service defaults.
- **SOTOPIA evaluator:** the pinned SOTOPIA v0.1.5 evaluator uses the fixed judge model after
  each episode; the model under evaluation never acts as its own judge.

When a judge call fails after retries, the sample is recorded as grader infrastructure
failure (counted against the run's error tolerance) rather than silently scored zero.

### Errors and Exceptions

#### Infrastructure Error Tolerance

Modern benchmarks are prone to encountering transient infrastructure errors. Our policy is to allow a degree of tolerance for infrastructure error; up to 10% of a benchmark's tasks can be invalidated by an infrastructure failure before we invalidate the entire score for a model on the benchmark. We do not attempt to control for the particular infrastructure errors that were encountered by various models on particular tasks. For this reason, we report confidence intervals as slightly wider than they would be if all models had reported on all tasks.

#### Infrastructure vs Model Error

We categorize errors during the evaluation process as either infrastructure errors or model errors.
Model errors are scoreable and do not count toward the infrastructure-error threshold. Unless this
policy explicitly identifies an error as a model error, it is an infrastructure error.

For Harbor evals, the following error types are currently treated as score-able model errors.

- `AgentTimeoutError`: the agent reached its configured execution timeout; Harbor preserves
  the work produced so far and runs the verifier.
- `ContextLengthExceededError`: the model or agent exhausted the available context; Harbor
  treats that as a classified end to the attempt and runs the verifier.
- `TurnCapExhaustedError`: the agent reached its configured turn cap without declaring
  completion; Harbor runs the verifier on the resulting state.
- `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`: the agent process exited non-zero after potentially producing
  scoreable work; Harbor still runs the verifier. Agent-specific subclasses must be reported
  under their concrete exception type and reviewed for validity rather than silently grouped.

For these Harbor score-able model errors, we terminate the trial and then run the verifier on the output of the agent, if any output is present. Unlike the Evalchemy timeout rule above, we do *not* automatically score Harbor model errors as 0's. This is because sometimes, agents will solve the task correctly and then get stuck in a loop of self-doubt or fail to submit properly in their harness, and we regard that outcome as closer to a success than a failure.

#### Timeout Policy

The following limits apply to every policy benchmark; there are no benchmark-specific exceptions.

| Evaluator phase | Limit | Outcome when the limit expires |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Evalchemy trial | 30 minutes | Record `0.0` as an `AgentTimeoutError`. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor agent setup | 6 minutes | Record `AgentSetupTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |
| Harbor agent execution | 30 minutes | Record `AgentTimeoutError`, preserve the agent's work, and run the verifier. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor verifier | 5 minutes | Record `VerifierTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |

The Evalchemy limit covers the full trial, including request retries and backoff, after the trial
acquires an evaluator slot. Evalchemy [#175](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/pull/175)
implements the deadline, and campaign configs set `timeout=1800`.

Harbor launch configs override task-manifest values with
`agents[].override_setup_timeout_sec: 360`, `agents[].override_timeout_sec: 1800`, and
`verifier.override_timeout_sec: 300`. `artifacts/common.sh` checks these values before submission,
so the same limits apply even when a task manifest omits its own timeout.

## Baseline Models

### How we select baseline models

The process for selecting baseline models in our policy is fundamentally heuristic and community-driven. For each new model release, we will strive to select a representative cohort of open-weights and open-source models that are roughly comparable to Marin models and document them in the policy. We will look up reported results for those models in the research literature and, where available, use them as targets for internal reproduction, noting, however, that typically the variance in hyperparameters will make published results not directly comparable to our own. We will sometimes substitute quantized variants of the listed models for the canonical models, especially for larger models where our hardware makes it challenging to run inference on the non-quantized variants.

## Eval launch commands (Marin)

These commands require access to the `marin` Iris controller and the `cw-rno2a` federated cluster.
Run them from the archived `artifacts/marin-checkout`; it is the experiment worktree based on the
pinned Marin branch. Set `MODEL` to an artifact filename stem. The standard and SOTOPIA launches
use `artifacts/model-configs/$MODEL.yaml`; the other agentic launches use the corresponding
`artifacts/model-configs/new-arms/$MODEL-pi.yaml`.

```bash
ARTIFACTS=/absolute/path/to/eval-policy-09-17/artifacts
MARIN="$ARTIFACTS/marin-checkout"
MODEL="REPLACE_WITH_MODEL_CONFIG_FILENAME_STEM"
STANDARD_MODEL_CONFIG="$ARTIFACTS/model-configs/$MODEL.yaml"
AGENTIC_MODEL_CONFIG="$ARTIFACTS/model-configs/new-arms/$MODEL-pi.yaml"

cd "$MARIN"
test "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" = 196137104ceb6d5cd0c634d1e840d4390c897b5a
uv sync --all-packages

export TOGETHER_API_KEY="REPLACE_WITH_TOGETHER_API_KEY"
export JUDGE_API_KEY="$TOGETHER_API_KEY"
export JUDGE_BASE_URL=https://api.together.xyz/v1
export JUDGE_MODEL=openai/gpt-oss-120b
export OPENAI_API_KEY="$TOGETHER_API_KEY"
export OPENAI_BASE_URL="$JUDGE_BASE_URL"
export TAU2_USER_MODEL=openai/openai/gpt-oss-120b
export TAU2_NL_ASSERTIONS_MODEL="$TAU2_USER_MODEL"

common=(--federated_cluster cw-rno2a
  --priority interactive --version eval-policy-updated)
standard=(uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch
  --model-config "$STANDARD_MODEL_CONFIG" "${common[@]}")
agentic=(uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch
  --model-config "$AGENTIC_MODEL_CONFIG" "${common[@]}")

"${standard[@]}" --evals \
  math500,humanevalplus,mbppplus,olympiadbench,gsm8k-0shot,piqa,winogrande,boolq,truthfulqa,triviaqa

# AIME24 campaign protocol: ten outer launches with no launcher seed override. Evalchemy's
# benchmark implementation generates ten internally seeded responses per question per launch.
for launch_index in $(seq 1 10); do
  "${standard[@]}" --evals aime24
done

"${standard[@]}" \
  --evalchemy-config "$ARTIFACTS/policy-configs/mmlu-pro.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$ARTIFACTS/policy-configs/gpqa-diamond.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$ARTIFACTS/policy-configs/cruxeval.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$ARTIFACTS/policy-configs/financebench.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$ARTIFACTS/policy-configs/ifbench.yaml" \
  --evalchemy-config "$ARTIFACTS/policy-configs/mrcr.yaml"
"${standard[@]}" --evalchemy-config "$ARTIFACTS/policy-configs/nupa-full.yaml"

for config in swebench-recovery ot-tblite-recovery tb2-recovery ds-1000-local \
              bfclparity-pi bixbench-pi tau3-pi; do
  "${agentic[@]}" --harbor-config "$ARTIFACTS/harbor-configs/$config.yaml"
done
"${standard[@]}" --harbor-config \
  "$MARIN/experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/sotopia-hard.yaml"
```

and Daytona sandboxes and served with the checkpoint, vLLM flags, topology, and sampling settings
in the matching artifact model YAML. `MODEL_BASE_URL` is the API root ending in `/v1`; `MODEL_ID`
must match the name returned by `/models`; `TOKENIZER_ID` is the Hugging Face repository and
`TOKENIZER_REVISION` its immutable revision. Evalchemy executes generated code for HumanEvalPlus
and MBPPPlus.

git clone https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy.git
cd evalchemy
