topics.title: Store Hero convolution history per request slot
topics.body:
Store Hero short-convolution history once per request slot and copy it when
requests are cloned. Persistent slot IDs preserve history across packed-batch
reordering, recycled prompts clear old state, and pages for an original prompt
are allocated before fully populated pages are shared with its clones.

For the current 48-layer configuration, the cache initializer reports that a
4096-token request with 128-token pages reduces logical BF16 history allocation
from 121.5 MiB to 3.796875 MiB. Focused CPU coverage exercises Hero clone
tokens/logprobs, queued slot reuse, and FP32/BF16 convolution parity.
Accelerator memory and latency remain unmeasured; replaying an earlier prompt
prefix after slot reuse still requires recomputation. See the [slot-history
tests](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9687/files). Builds on
[#9659](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9659).

topics.title: [grug] Add hero launch controls for a context-length switch
topics.body:
The scaling-ladder launcher holds 4,194,304 tokens per rack per update, so the sequence batch shrinks as the context grows (2816 sequences at 16K on 11 racks). The step count (390251), learning rates, decay, and gate/router weight decay therefore match the 4K run. The hero's context length, QK multipliers, and capacity factor live in HERO_MODEL. --qk-mult and --qk-mult-long-scale (global layers only) override the QK multipliers for trial arms and ladder rungs; trial arms set the context length on their branch alongside the history. Eval packs at the training context, as on main, so the eval_dropless/* series shift at each switch. For short trial arms, --eval-every overrides the eval cadence.

The hero's context history is checked in, like the data mix's switch point: HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES in launch_scaling_ladder.py lists each context the d6144 hero trained at before its current one with the step it ended at, and HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL holds the parent's cumulative training FLOPs at the last switch. A context-switch deploy PR edits Python only: it sets the HERO_MODEL fields, appends one entry to HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES, and sets HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL, so a second switch (4K to 16K, then 16K to 64K) is described exactly and trigger_hero.sh is unchanged. The launcher turns the history into a FlopsBaseline at the last end step and, through the prior_context_phases argument of harrier_mix_2026_08_18_data_config, into LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases, with each earlier phase's Harrier stage schedule and shuffle blocks at its own batch size, so the Harrier sources continue from their earlier reads. At d6144 the launcher rejects a history that does not start at 4K, repeats a length between adjacent phases (including the current context), or disagrees with whether the baseline is set. LmDataConfig rejects end steps that do not increase, and rejects any switch below the 1e23-FLOP simulated-epoching cutoff because the data offsets assume each source reads its whole cache. The narrow rungs take no history.

The live run is unchanged: trigger_hero.sh is identical to main and launches the 4K HERO_MODEL with no FLOPs baseline. A switch still needs a GPU rehearsal from the handoff checkpoint and agreed trial thresholds; see the inventory and validation plan in #9615.

topics.title: Time experiment graph setup and isolate Levanter training imports
topics.body:
Report experiment graph construction and execution setup durations, and make training checkpoint types importable without Levanter. Training functions are defined in `marin.training.levanter`; callers import those functions directly from that module. Checkpoint, metrics and pod configuration classes are defined in `marin.training.training`. Existing artifact records identify their result type as `marin.training.training.LevanterCheckpoint`. That class stays at its recorded path so those artifacts load without `ArtifactTypeMismatchError`.

The CatCount RL canary launcher (`python -m experiments.post_training.cat_count_canary`) imports `marin.rl.skyrl` to submit training to Iris. Both import checkpoint types from `marin.training.training`. Importing either the launcher or `marin.rl.skyrl` loads no Levanter, Transformers, Torch or W&B module. On October 15, `python -X importtime -c 'import marin.rl.skyrl'` reported 22.19 seconds on main and 4.24 seconds on this branch (one fresh interpreter each; cache warmth was not controlled). These are local import measurements; coordinator startup in Iris has not been measured.

Commands using `marin.experiment.cli` configure INFO logging when the root logger has no handlers. Their INFO log messages report elapsed graph-construction time as `experiment/build`, including when printing a plan without `--run`. With `--run`, `marin.execution.lazy.run` also times provenance collection and graph lowering once per call (`execution/provenance`, `execution/lower`), and dependency expansion for each requested step (`execution/expand`). [RL startup design](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/596). Outside Iris, `--run` on an RL command built with `marin.rl.cli`, such as the CatCount launcher, submits an Iris coordinator job that reruns the command; the `execution/*` messages appear in that job's log.

`lib/iris` requires `marin-iris-native` 0.1.13.dev38952644761 or later. Its public proxy applies an identity's `auth.user_roles` entry before `auth.admin_users` and the default role, matching the Python role policy.

For dense Qwen, a test imports `marin.rl.cli` in a fresh interpreter and fails if Levanter, Transformers, Torch or W&B is loaded; a separate fresh-interpreter import of `experiments.post_training.cat_count_canary.launcher` on October 16 at `0393bc96` loaded none of them. Snowball and Hero launchers import training functions, such as `resolve_training_env` and `run_levanter_train_lm`, from `marin.training.levanter`, and checkpoint and configuration records from `marin.training.training`. Every class and function in those two modules has the same AST as in main's `marin.training.training`, so Snowball and Hero need no model-specific numerical check for these import and timing changes.

topics.title: [eval] Run each evaluation as a StepSpec
topics.body:
Run each evaluation as a StepSpec with its own lock, success cache, and result record. Evaluations in one launch share a candidate server and optional hosted judge. Cached evaluations are skipped on restart; a fully cached launch starts no servers. A group StepSpec locks the launch before starting inference so duplicate orchestrators cannot provision duplicate servers.

Evaluators run sequentially by default. `--max-concurrent` allows concurrent evaluators on shared inference, but omits per-evaluation server metrics because server-wide counters include sibling traffic. Server startup failures write infrastructure-failure records for all pending evaluations.

Pipeline retries derive run IDs from the pipeline artifact path and resolved model, evaluator, runtime, judge, and policy settings, preserving completed evaluations across orchestrator resubmissions. CLI launches and mutable pipeline versions (`dev` or `*-dev`) create fresh runs. Verified policies retain their pinned benchmark sources and Harbor/Evalchemy commits.

EvalDash withholds scores until each evaluation's StepSpec succeeds. Historical records without step status keep their existing display. A crash after writing a record but before StepRunner marks success can rerun that evaluation. The success cache prevents completed steps from being overwritten on ordinary restarts, addressing the failure in the [October 6 incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/627).

topics.title: [taskforge] Run each item through a resumable loop with an event log
topics.body:
`taskforge.loop` carries one capability idea to proposals and each proposal to a terminal:
`ACCEPTED`, `REJECTED`, `ABANDONED` or `FAILED`. `run_idea` proposes a batch; a failed slot costs
only that slot, and only a batch with no proposals is re-proposed, up to `max_idea_reproposals`.
`run_item` runs triage with bounded rubric repairs, authoring and building with bounded revisions
(the revision loop that lived in an evidence script), control replay, solver and adversary trials,
the calibration summary and review's decision. A `Repair` starts the next round: the author revises
the condemned program with the brief as `Revision.failure`, and the build recomputes the steps the
repair invalidates. A `Retry` waits out the policy backoff, without holding a slot, and re-runs only
the unsettled trials; spent retries end the item `ABANDONED`. An unhandled exception records
`FAILED` and propagates.

Item status is a fold over `EntryKind.EVENT` ledger rows, never a stored file. Each sub-phase
appends one completion event to the item's JSONL log (and, under Iris, to the Finelog mirror), with
a contiguous per-item `seq` and a schema version; `derive_state` raises on a gap, a repeat or an
unknown schema, which is how a second process writing the same run root shows up. A draft is keyed by
`task_digest(draft.lowered)`, which covers the answer format the TaskSpec carries. A relaunch re-runs only the sub-phase without its
completion event: build steps are memoized, settled trials load from
their attempt files, and review is pure. `ABANDONED` and `FAILED` items re-enter on the next launch,
an abandoned one at the control replay with a fresh retry budget, or at the build it was abandoned
in with a fresh host-failure count. A log opened under a different `policy.json` is refused.

The run root keeps what produced each item, not only its outcome. `run_idea` writes the consumer's
idea record once to `items/idea--<id>/idea.json` (`LoopServices.describe_idea`) and every proposal
batch under `items/idea--<id>/batches/<reproposal>/`: the planning request, its completions and the
slot plan, and per slot the request, the completions and `repair_error.txt` or `failure.txt`.
`OPENED` records `origin`, `generated` for a proposal from a batch and `supplied` for one handed to
`run_item` directly, so a viewer can tell a live test's fixed proposal from a generated one.

`LoopPolicy` states every bound with no defaults, including the validation deadlines
(`total_turn_timeout`, `attempt_timeout`), and `POLICY` reads it from `policy.json`, rejecting
a missing or unknown key at any depth. Build revisions and review repairs are separate bounds because
a revision costs one author call and a repair costs a validation round. A rebuild that produces the
same task digest after a repair counts as a failed revision whose failure text repeats the brief,
so the author cannot spend the repair budget returning the same program. The output-token budget
sums the item's `LLM_CALL` entries, including the triage calls the loop records, and is checked
before each authoring. Validation trials also record their model calls in the item ledger under
steps `solver/<index>` and `adversary/<role>/<index>`; the budget leaves those out
(`loop.events.UNBUDGETED_TRIALS`), since `k`, `adversary_k`, the verifier submission budget and the
deadlines bound them. The exclusion requires the `/`, so a build step that happens to be named
`solver` or `adversary` still counts. A build failure or any exception the builder program raises
goes back to the author; `GlmUnavailable` propagates instead, since no revision fixes the endpoint.

A build the machine host failed is neither. `builder.infrastructure.BuildInfrastructureFailure` (no
factory for a machine backend, no image builder, a scheduling timeout, an unreachable host) spends no
revision and never reaches the author. The loop records a `BUILD_INFRASTRUCTURE` event, waits out the retry backoff and
rebuilds the same program; a host failure after `max_build_retries` rebuilds ends the item
`ABANDONED` with its cause counts. A cause in `builder.infrastructure.HOST_REJECTIONS` (no factory for
a machine backend, no image builder) holds for as long as the host is unchanged, so it abandons the
item at once without a retry. It is not a `HOST` rejection: `REJECTED` is final, and a run root moved to a host
with the factory must still build the item. A host failure never ends an item `REJECTED` or
`FAILED`. `loop.events.build_host_failures` counts an item's host failures for the queue report.

Band handling is the consumer's choice. `LoopPolicy.band_rules` is review's `BandRules`: per band
kind (too easy, too hard) the repairs a task outside the band gets and, once they are spent, whether
it is accepted or rejected. `ItemState.band_repairs` counts the repairs each kind has had. An accept's
`DECIDED` event carries `band` and the synthesis pass rate (`solved`, `graded`, `solve_rate`), and
its `TERMINAL` reason is `calibrated` or `accepted outside the band: <band>`, so a log tells the two
apart without opening `decision.json`.

Adversary trials are verifier agent loops on the run's `GlmClient`, briefed with the consumer's
`LoopServices.adversary_context` for the item's proposal. `ADVERSARIES_RUN` counts per role the
graded trials, the passing ones, their verifier submissions and their `SHORTCUT` claims
(`trial_claim`), and records `context_digest`, the sha256 of the consumer's context. `DECIDED` names
the kinds of the passes graded NOTED in its `notes` attr, so a run's logs show the adversary results
that were recorded but not repaired.

The live test hands a stored d43 culinary-scaling proposal to `run_item` as a supplied proposal on
the GLM-5.3 interactive pool under k=8, adversary_k=2, 10 verifier submissions with a repair
threshold of 3, band [0.125, 0.875] and Taskforge's own band rules (one repair per kind, then
reject). It requires `ACCEPTED` or `REJECTED` with a `decision.json` for every `DECIDED` event, the
adversary's system turn in every adversary attempt file, and a relaunch that returns the same
terminal without a model call. The unit programs build a ShellSim task whose Python grader runs in a verifier
machine on the ShellSim-backed fixture factory, lowered with `b.lower`. On this base the live loop
test took a proposal through build, validation and review to a terminal in 19 minutes.

Stacks on #9848.

topics.title: [grug] Add a Triton flash attention for AMD GPUs
topics.body:
Add `gpu_triton_flash`, an opt-in fused causal attention for Grug on AMD GPUs, where Grug had no fused kernel. Existing backends are unchanged. The forward, dQ and dK/dV kernels are Triton kernels launched through `jax_triton`, like the top-k and Sonic MoE kernels. Earlier revisions of this PR used the Pallas Triton backend. JAX 0.11 deprecates it and tells Triton users to switch to the official Triton bindings and `jax_triton`; its other route, Pallas on Mosaic GPU, does not target AMD GPUs.

The kernels reduce each mask to one inclusive key lower bound per query, `max(segment start, q - W + 1)` for window `W`. Key blocks outside `[lower bound, q]` are skipped, and blocks fully inside it skip the mask computation. GQA indexes the shared KV head instead of repeating K/V, for any ratio that divides the heads. The dK/dV kernel computes `K Qᵀ`, so P and dS come out of their matmuls already transposed for the dV and dK matmuls. Under a mesh, including Grug's one-device mesh, the kernels run inside `shard_map`; batch and heads may be sharded, sequence and head_dim may not.

One layer's forward plus backward at the June model's per-GPU shape (8 x 4096 tokens, 20 query heads, 5 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16), median of three interleaved rounds in one process (jobs 457836, 457837):

| Mask | GPU | reference | Pallas Triton (earlier revision) | `gpu_triton_flash` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| window 2048 | MI350X | 20.19 ms | 6.77 ms | 5.11 ms |
| causal | MI350X | 22.26 ms | 10.04 ms | 8.38 ms |
| window 2048 | MI300X | 31.17 ms | 12.04 ms | 10.17 ms |
| causal | MI300X | 32.32 ms | 17.28 ms | 15.25 ms |

Pallas hands its Triton IR to XLA's bundled Triton, while `jax_triton` compiles with pip triton 3.6. With the Pallas revision's tiles, the port ran 11-13% slower than Pallas, so the tiles were swept again on both GPUs. MI350X (gfx950) runs the forward with two pipeline stages and MI300X with one; the other tiles are shared.

Value and gradient parity tests against `reference_attention` pass on MI300X and MI350X. CI has neither a GPU nor jax-triton, so it skips them. All dots run at IEEE precision: by default Triton runs float32 dots as xf32 on MI300X, which failed the float32 tests. Float32 inputs get smaller tiles, because the bf16 tiles overflow MI300X's 64 KiB of shared memory.

On ROCm the kernels need jaxlib 0.11.1 or newer with jax-triton 0.3.1 and triton 3.6; jaxlib 0.11.0 never loads `jax_rocm10_plugin`'s Triton launcher. The measurements above used jax 0.11.1, jax_rocm10_plugin 0.11.1+rocm10.1.0, jax-triton 0.3.1 and triton 3.6.0. #9989 moves the HPC Fund venv recipe to these versions.

Each run of equal segment IDs is one document, so a segment ID that reappears after a different ID starts a new document; `reference_attention` lets the two runs attend to each other. Masks that carry FA4 precomputed bounds, as moe_hero_ep and moe_hero_fsdp build them, supply the lower bounds directly; padding queries then attend only to themselves.

jax-triton kernels fail today when one process drives several AMD GPUs: on a kernel's first launch, jaxlib 0.11.1 reads the compiled hsaco from a temporary file and deletes it without holding its cache lock, so all but one GPU fail and the step stalls at the next collective (repro in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9853#issuecomment-6090140907). #10014 lands the Pallas-Triton version of these kernels in the meantime; this PR replaces it once AMD's jax fork fixes the race.

Part of #9812
topics.head: 600e47a4af1b57f1910f1ddae3145a8c78177408

topics.title: [haliax] Add tile-map Triton ragged_dot kernels for AMD Instinct GPUs
topics.body:
Do not merge yet: on ROCm, jaxlib 0.11.1 races when the GPUs of one process first launch the same jax-triton kernel, and an 8-GPU training step with these kernels hangs at its first collective. The cause and evidence are below; merging waits for a jaxlib fix. Until then, #10009 lands the Pallas-Triton version of these kernels, and this PR replaces it.

On AMD Instinct GPUs, `ragged_dot(..., implementation="triton")` now runs a second family of grouped-GEMM kernels, called tile-map kernels, written in Triton and launched through `jax_triton.triton_call` as Grug's routing top-k (#9942) is. JAX 0.11 deprecates the Pallas-Triton backend, and Mosaic GPU, the replacement JAX suggests, does not support ROCm. AMD Instinct GPUs use the tile-map kernels when jax-triton imports, which on ROCm needs jaxlib 0.11.1, and fall back to the group-grid kernels otherwise. NVIDIA GPUs, TPU and megablox behave exactly as before. NVIDIA keeps the existing Pallas-Triton group-grid kernels and block sizes, including the Blackwell `block_n` of 256. `_TILE_MAP_GPU_FAMILIES` lists the GPU families that use the tile-map kernels. Adding NVIDIA to it is a one-line change, for a follow-up once H100 and B200 have been measured.

The existing kernels give every group a full grid over all row tiles and exit early on most of them. In the tile-map kernels, the forward and input-gradient (dlhs) kernels launch one program per (group, row tile, column tile) from a tile map built on device from `group_sizes`, as in megablox's `make_group_metadata`. dlhs reads the weights transposed in place, with no `rhs.mT` copy. The weight gradient (drhs) uses one flat grid over all groups and reads its lhs tile transposed. Rows past `sum(group_sizes)` are zero-filled. The old kernels leave them unwritten. Block sizes come from a per-GPU-family table swept on MI350X. Two launch-order options are new: chiplet-aware program numbering (`num_xcds`) and grouped tile rows (`group_m`).

Per-call times on one MI350X, bf16, balanced groups. Each cell is TFLOP/s for the old kernels, then the new ones (job 457866). The June expert shapes are G=32, with w13 at K=N=2560 and w2 at K=1280, N=2560.

| Shape | M | fwd | dlhs | drhs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| June w13 | 16384 | 95 → 621 | 88 → 632 | 382 → 506 |
| June w13 | 131072 | 598 → 784 | 570 → 806 | 433 → 689 |
| June w13 | 196608 | 542 → 800 | 526 → 826 | 435 → 707 |
| June w2 | 131072 | 569 → 725 | 555 → 764 | 415 → 639 |
| Mixtral-like w1, G=8, 4096x14336 | 16384 | 423 → 815 | 383 → 864 | 443 → 756 |
| Mixtral-like w1 | 65536 | 633 → 857 | 601 → 907 | 457 → 777 |

A dense `jnp.matmul` with the same FLOPs runs at about 730-960 TFLOP/s on this GPU.

An earlier revision of this PR wrote the tile-map kernels in Pallas-Triton. At every shape above, the jax-triton kernels return outputs bitwise identical to that version on MI350X and MI300X (jobs 457866, 457867). XLA compiles Pallas-Triton kernels with its bundled Triton, while jax-triton uses pip triton 3.6, and with the same block config the jax-triton drhs kernel ran 29-33% slower on MI350X. Reading the lhs tile transposed and a new drhs sweep (job 457862) fixed that: 256x256x64 blocks with 8 warps and 2 stages reach at least 94% of the best of 272 configurations at each of five shapes. Against the Pallas-Triton version, drhs now runs 4-30% faster on MI350X and 31-76% faster on MI300X, fwd 2-8% faster and dlhs up to 2% slower on MI350X, and fwd and dlhs within 3% on MI300X. The fwd and dlhs entries are the ones swept with the Pallas-Triton version.

On ROCm, jax-triton hands jaxlib the path of a temporary hsaco file. On a kernel's first launch, `GetModuleImage` in `jaxlib/gpu/triton_kernels.cc` misses its cache, then reads the file and deletes it without holding its lock. When the 8 device threads of one process launch a new kernel together, all but one fail with `/tmp/tmp...; No such file or directory` and skip the rest of the step, and the others wait at the next collective until XLA aborts. In the June model on 8x MI350X with EP8, recompute_all and batch 64, any one of the three layouts on jax-triton triggers it (job 457945). A gdb breakpoint on `XlaCustomCallStatusSetFailure` caught the error (job 457957), and strace showed the 8 threads unlinking the same file within 0.3 ms (job 457961). Other jax-triton kernels in multi-GPU ROCm runs hit the same race, including #9942's top-k. The fix belongs in jaxlib: compile under the lock, or stop deleting the file. With the Pallas-Triton version of these kernels, the same step took 2.420 s against 2.627 s with the group-grid kernels (job 457874, reference attention).

The edge-case tests (empty groups, unaligned boundaries, rows past the last group, partial tiles, every VJP layout) run for both families on a GPU. All 88 pass on MI350X (job 457875). On MI300X, 58 pass and the 30 f32 cases skip, because Triton runs f32 dots in TF32 on gfx942 as it does on NVIDIA (job 457876). The tile-map kernels no longer run on CPU, so a CPU test checks that the tile map assigns every row to exactly one tile of its group. The per-call numbers and block sweeps come from `lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_ragged_dot_triton.py`, which is in #9894, stacked on this PR.

Background and earlier measurements: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6027367267

topics.title: [grug] Run the production hero with a PGLE latency profile
topics.body:
The hero's step is about 1.5-1.9% shorter with a PGLE (profile-guided latency estimation) profile, and production does not use one yet. The hero schedules with one collective in flight, and XLA's default latency estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so the scheduler treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under a single GEMM. A profile built from the program's own trace replaces those estimates with measured costs.

All four runs below are on the same 64-GPU rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps); the same code ran 0.8% faster on another rack, so only same-rack comparisons count.

| Program | No profile | Own profile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack #9830-#9836 with #9835, plus #9829 | 12.695 s | 12.506 s (+1.51%) |
| The same without #9835 | 12.763 s | 12.522 s (+1.92%) |

With a profile, #9835's hand-placed transport ordering was worth 0.13% (12.506 against 12.522 s), so #9835 was closed and its scheduling left to PGLE. Without a profile it was worth 0.54%, which production gives up until it runs with one.

`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/pgle_profile.py` (#9831) builds a profile from one XProf trace, and the hero README describes the trace, build and rerun loop. Automatic PGLE (`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE`) cannot profile with one process per GPU. A profile matches instructions by name, so it applies only to the program it was traced from: production needs a profile traced on its own 11-rack mesh, rebuilt after any change to the model, mesh or XLA flags. A stale profile loses the gain without an error.

Done when: the production hero runs with a profile built from its own program, the launcher warns or fails when the profile does not match the compiled program, and the production step-time change is recorded here.

Part of #9636.

topics.title: [levanter] Continue mixture reads across a context-length switch
topics.body:
Harrier's shuffle blocks change from a fixed 256 sequences to a fixed 2^20 tokens (io_block_size = 2**20 // seq_len). At 4K the two are identical, so the live run's data order is unchanged. At a longer context, the token-sized blocks keep the outer block permutation the same, and only the order of sequences inside each 512-block shuffle window changes. With the old 256-sequence blocks, a 16K relaunch would have re-read an estimated 2.85T already-seen tokens of the remaining ~9T.

The new LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases describes the earlier context lengths of a resumed run, one ContextPhaseConfig per length. With prior_context_phases set, each source skips the unread rest of the shuffle window it was reading at the switch step and starts its next window, so nothing is served twice. At a 216000-step handoff this skips about 52B tokens, 0.65% of the rest of the run. MixtureDataset takes per-source start offsets to apply the skip. Every phase must give positive weight to the same sources, because a training config drops zero-weight sources and that changes the shuffle keys of the rest; a change in the active sources is rejected. So is a phase at the same sequence length as the one before it, since there a source could continue in place and the skip would only discard data. The seed, the source order, and restoring at the last switch step cannot be checked from the config, so the field docstring states them. The offsets come from each source's true position in the earlier phase, so they also absorb the main-mixture boundary moving from step 108000 to 108096 at 16K. The grug train loop builds its mixture through the new LmDataConfig.train_mixture.

topics.title: [rl] Select PivotRL pivots from frozen-policy pass rates
topics.body:
This PR implements a few of the key components from the NVIDIA's [PivotRL paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.21383).

**PivotRL in a nutshell:**
1. make a bunch of `(trajectory, turn): (context up to turn) -> teacher action` tuples (I usually call this `long` or `melted` format).
2. generate `k` roll-outs from a frozen student at each of those points
3. grade them using "functional" verifiers
4. identify "pivot" turns -- ones that have non-zero reward variance and are meaningfully difficult
5. (... single-turn RL...)
6. ???
7. profit

**This PR is split into 4 commits, I recommend reviewing in that manner.**
1. add original nemotron graders
2. add datasets, initial data pre-processing and prediction code
3. prediction post-processing/filtering
4. add openhands dataset & grader for a novel experiment (I added this separately, to give a flavor for what it's like adding a new pivotRL task--tbd if any of this helps).

### Agent Generated

Build PivotRL's training data in Marin as artifact steps: candidates, pass rates under a frozen policy, then the pivots that Eq. 5 of the PivotRL paper selects (0 < passed < K and pass rate below λ), written as `train.parquet` in the candidate schema. Each λ and selection criterion is a small artifact over the same pass rates.

Candidates come from three releases. `marin.rl.nemotron_pivot` turns NVIDIA's SWE and Terminal pivot releases into one candidate per expert turn of each trajectory's longest row, keeping earlier turns' reasoning as `reasoning_content` and dropping NVIDIA's pass-rate fields; `experiments/datasets/nemotron_pivot.py` publishes them as `processed/nemotron-pivot-{swe,terminal}-long`. Validation holds out whole SWE instances (100) and Terminal tasks (30) by hash bucket and keeps four evenly spaced turns per held-out trajectory, about 500 rows each, since a trajectory's rows share almost their whole prompt. OpenHands candidates are prepared from `nebius/SWE-rebench-openhands-trajectories@3545538`: one row per expert tool call in a resolved trajectory, with the working directory replayed from earlier bash observations.

`marin.rl.pass_rates.measure_pass_rates` serves the policy with vLLM, sends one `n=K` chat request per row so each prompt is prefilled once, and grades every reply with a `PassRateTask` returning a verifyit `Reward`. Every grading component is its own column (`c_<name>` per sample, `passed_<name>` per row), so selection can switch criterion without resampling. Context overflows, persistent request failures, and grader errors exclude a row rather than scoring it 0. Rows commit in atomic chunks, so a rerun samples only missing chunks, and `config.json` refuses to resume under a different config. Every run sets `enable_thinking` explicitly: SWE and Terminal think, matching prompts that carry the teacher's reasoning; OpenHands does not, since its teacher never thinks. Grug runs keep special tokens so graders can strip its `<|start_think|>` block.

The graders live in verifyit. `nemotron_pivot.grade_tool_call` scores SWE replies with NeMo Gym's word-overlap argument match (the reward), the PivotRL paper's tool-name-only match, and an exact-argument match. `grade_terminus` ports the string-only Terminus-2 verifier, parsing the reply after any reasoning. `openhands_next_action` grades by what a call does and to which paths, so `cat core.py` from the package directory matches viewing `widgets/core.py`; pairs the rules cannot settle go to an LLM judge only when one is configured. MarinSkyRL computes training rewards with the same algorithms but pins the standalone verifyit repository, so sharing these graders there needs that pin moved to `lib/verifyit`.

This replaces profiling inside MarinSkyRL's generate entrypoint, which reached 63-79 samples/min on 16 H100s while vLLM ran 2-10 of 16 sequences, because each request group waited on single-writer trajectory retention.

Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05 smoke runs on one 8xH100 node each, the first 64 candidates per dataset and K=8 (seed 1), graded all 1,536 replies with no exclusions:

| dataset | thinking | replies that think | passes / 512 | pivots |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SWE | on | 462 | 113 (tool name only: 264) | 24 |
| Terminal | on | 181 | 20 | 9 |
| OpenHands | off | 0 | 280 | 40 |

On SWE, the prompt length vLLM reports is within 10 tokens of a local render that includes earlier reasoning and about 490 tokens above one without it, so the reasoning reaches the model; Terminal and OpenHands match exactly. Grug's thinking never leaks into tool-call arguments.

topics.title: [grug] Prepare the hero handoff to the MoE optimization stack
topics.body:
Hand the hero off from `hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k` to `hero-mfu30-step231k`, which runs main with the MoE optimization stack (#9829–#9834) and the launch memory settings from #9958. The new run continues from checkpoint 231464, forced on the old run, marked non-temporary, and copied to `s3://hero-checkpoints/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-231464`. Its W&B run forks from the old run at `_step` 231463.

On one GB200 NVL72 rack restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint, the stack trains 4K sequences at 12.70 s/step against 13.97 s/step before it (30.9% against 28.1% MFU), with peak HBM 124.0 GiB against an allocator limit of 143.8 GiB. 8K and 16K speed up by 10.0% and 9.6% with unchanged expert-drop fractions. The d768 validation `validate9885-d768-20261008` tracked `validate9378-d768-20260923` over 11,420 steps: final held-out loss 2.6783 against 2.6791, routing unchanged, and training loss 6.3e-4 lower on average ([report](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/x--VmlldzoxODA3OTE2Mg==)). Single-rack runs do not exercise the 11-rack collectives, so the 200-step paired trial after cutover is the first multi-rack test.

prompts.text:
Was reading "Lost in Backpropagation: The LM Head is a Gradient Bottleneck" by @nthngdy and @yoavartzi the other day. Their ideas seemed very clever, but my ability to follow their intuition was lacking. So I decided to imagine "What would it be like to work as a neuron", to better process their ideas. The main audience when writing this was just myself. Sharing in case others find it a fun read.

A Day in the Life of a Neuron Associate at Grub Zoo.
prompts.expected:
Welcome to Grub Zoo. Proud home of 1000 animals. Each animal has its own designated 5 minute feeding window during the day where it eats one serving of grub. The feeding schedule looks something like:
-Feed the horse and the Giraffe from 4:00-4:05.
-Feed the rhino from 4:15-4:20.
-Feed the 8 alligators from 7:10-7:15.

Initially the Zoo ran off a simple lookup chart, where one could query a 5 minute window, and get returned a list of all animals that needed to be fed. Well, Bob from Marketing had a great (terrible) idea to replace our lookup table with AI. But instead of using AI, we could just become AI (wtf?). He explained that we’d each get some role in a mega human neural network, then use the power of ‘backpropagation’ to tell each other what to do. I think this is his promo project or something, not sure. His idea is that the optimal feeding window should depend on all sorts of properties of the weather, and once we get this learning machine running, it can plug in a bunch of these advanced features.

The first part of the plan was to designate 10 employees as feeders. Each feeder had to write down how they would divvy up any grub they were given between the 1,000 animals. One feeder, Jeremy, decided he’d give all grub he was given to the sloth. Weird guy. Another one, Anna, decided she’d split up the grub equally across all 1,000 animals. (How’s she gonna manage that, lol?).

My job was the supplier. Every 5 minutes I’d show up with some servings of grub. Then I’d have to divvy it up between the feeders, who’d then divvy it up between the animals based on their prearranged fractions. The weird part here is that I was the only one who was aware of the time of day- the feeders always stuck to their fractions.

Bob said that during each 5 minute interval we’d have two phases: an execution phase, and a feedback phase. Well for the first 5 minute execution phase I frankly had no idea what was going on, so I just gave an equal amount of grub to each of the 10 feeders, who then distributed it out. Somehow Anna was able to get grub out to all 1,000 animals, impressive.

Only the horse and the giraffe were supposed to get fed in this window, but the small amount of grub ended up spread out across all animals, and nobody was happy. I voted to drop Bob’s idea, but he figured we could salvage things. His insight was “Most windows only have a couple animals who need getting fed, so after everybody distributes their grub, we should apply some sort of bunching action towards the ones with the most grub. That way at least somebody gets a decent meal. Sometimes multiple animals need grub and we won’t be sure we got it right, so just do soft bunching.” He called it softmax.

We applied his technique, and sure enough one animal got a good meal, but it was the wrong animal! And the animals at Grub Zoo are extremely picky about when they get fed! Well, Bob said this was ok at first (what?), we just needed the feedback phase.

The feedback phase started with the animals. The ones that didn’t get fed but were supposed to, complained loudly. The feeders were the only ones who could observe and hear the animals. Each feeder would first go observe all 1000 animals to see which ones were complaining. Then they’d update their fractions slightly towards giving them more grub. Now if the supplier had given the feeder little or no grub that window, the feeder would take little effort in updating their fraction as it wouldn’t matter anyway. But if they had been given a large amount of grub, they’d take tremendous honor in updating their fraction quite heavily. But they had to be careful here! They were going to use that fraction for every time window, so they didn’t want to over-correct for one 5 minute interval.

The next phase of feedback was for me as the supplier. Each of the 10 feeders came and told me either ‘Man I coulda made a difference I had the fractions right just give me more grub’, or ‘I was off on this one, didn’t need grub here’. Then my job was to update ‘Ok for this 5 minute interval, give grub to feeder X’, because they told me their fraction is calibrated. I figured none of the feeders had it exactly right, but if I gave more grub to the feeders that seemed decent at the right times, their errors would average out and softmax would help bunch it up on the right animals.

To me the process felt pretty dumb, as the feeders were just like mindless cogs, trying to find the one right fraction. They could see all 1000 animals. But all I could see were 10 people shouting ‘give me more/less grub’. And somehow I was supposed to manage all the windows from that?

Over time I developed a massive lookup table. For each 5 minute interval, how much grub to give to each of the 10 feeders. Each feeder started to get more sophisticated specialization. For instance, one guy fed just the 8 alligators. I knew to only give him grub from 7:10-7:15, because that’s when he complained.

Well, Bob got wind that I was using a lookup table for each 5 minute window and freaked out. Said it wasn’t true AI. Said I was getting demoted to a neuron. 9 other people got hired as neurons too, working in parallel to me.

Now instead of a unique fraction for each window, I had a simpler role. I had to learn a fixed ratio across the 10 feeders, and a simple rule for when to switch on. Initially I just put the fraction on for the morning. And then tuned the fraction a bit to give grub to the feeders that were clamoring for more grub in the morning. I figured if I helped focus on some of the morning intervals, other ‘neuron associates’ could manage other windows of the day. I never got to see what these other neuron associates were up to, but I figured if I listened to the feeders I could help compensate for the gaps.

Well, we got some new funding, and Bob decided to hire some more ‘neuron associates’, so we are up to 20 now. Communication is becoming a real problem. We never talk to each other, and it’s getting kind of weird only listening to the 10 feeders and trying to compensate for what all my coworkers are doing.

Now Bob had the craziest idea yet. He decided to break up our 20 neuron associates into two 10 member squads: Alpha and Bravo. I got put on Bravo. During each interval I’d get to see both the time of day, and how much the Alpha Squad was planning to give to each feeder. I decided to take on a targeted role: IF the time was between 10-11am AND I saw that Alpha Squad was giving grub to feeder 2, then I’d give grub to feeder 1 and 2. I learned that in the morning whenever Alpha Squad gave grub to feeder 2, feeder 2 would still complain and want even more, and feeder 1 complained as well.

I noticed that sometimes Alpha Squad would slip up and not give grub to feeder 2, which meant I didn’t trigger on feeder 1 or 2. When this happened, I’d complain loudly. Hey Alpha! Give more grub to feeder 2! Problem is, team Alpha was getting overwhelmed during the feedback cycle. They had to listen to both the feeders directly, and every single member on squad Bravo. The problem got even worse when we doubled the size of Alpha and Bravo to 20 people each. That’s when Bob started hiring a new role, called ‘transporters’ and ‘messengers’.

There was one messenger and transporter for each feeder. Everyone only got to receive feedback from the messengers, and give grub to the transporters. During the execution phase, the transporters would collect the grub from squad Alpha, then I could make my decision based on if transporter 2 had grub. All of us in squad Bravo would then add on to the grub the transporters were carrying. During the feedback phase, I’d tell messenger 2 if I wanted more grub sent to feeder 2. This way, Alpha squad didn’t have to talk to both the feeders and Bravo squad. The messengers just added up the feedback from both the feeders and Bravo.

We ran this operation for several weeks, with Alpha and Bravo squads distributing grub to the transporters, the messengers giving feedback, and the feeders divvying it out and observing the animals. It seemed like the dumbest thing I’d ever seen! A lookup table could have done the same thing!

Well, that’s when Bob made a change that actually blew my mind. He called it the ‘magic of generalization’. The first thing he did was give all neuron associates access to the temperature, in addition to the time of day. Now in the old world, we’d have to manually make updates to all 1000 animals in the lookup table to figure out how they responded to temperature. In the new world, I only had to change my allocation to the 10 transporters. The feeders had already built fractions that grouped the animals into correlated sets.

I developed a new trigger condition. IF the time was between 10-11am AND transporter 2 had grub AND the temperature was above 60F, then give grub to transporter 1, 2, and 3. I came to learn that in very cold weather, these messengers didn’t complain as much.

Over time Bob added new features I could trigger on. Rain. Wind. Sunshine. It was starting to be quite a lot to handle. Bob always had to go around explaining to every neuron associate how this new measurement would work. Eventually Bob got pretty tired of this. He decided that only squad Alpha could see things like time, temperature, rain, wind, and sunshine. At first this seemed completely crazy to me. How could I know when to trigger, without these key features?

We concocted a pretty funny plan. I noticed that messenger 9 NEVER complained. My guess is that feeder 9 was just completely checked-out. Never gave any grub to anyone. Team Alpha had picked up on this. They also knew that whenever it was between 10-11am and above 60F, messenger 2 would complain to them. So they decided to give grub to transporter 9 whenever it got hot in the morning- not because transporter 9 needed the grub. But because team Bravo could then use that signal to make better decisions.

I developed a new heuristic: IF transporter 2 AND transporter 9 have grub, then we give grub to transporter 1,2,3. AND we also take that grub away from transporter 9 and add it to the pile, since feeder 9 never complains.

So that became my job. I’d wake up every morning, drive in to work as a neuron associate, then pay very close attention to which 10 transporters had grub, and how that correlated to the complaints I’d get from the 10 messengers. I’d update my fractions among the 10 transporters, and update my feedback to the 10 messengers.

Later that month my team name got updated to Squad Bravo-46. What the heck? Turns out Bob had really scaled the operation. We now had 50 Bravo squads in series. My job was always the same, talk to 10 messengers, and observe 10 transporters. I had no idea what measurements got fed into Alpha Squad. And honestly, I had no idea how many animals even lived at the Zoo anymore. I didn’t even know how many team members were on Bravo-46, since I never talked to them.

Alpha Squad was the only team that got to see the pure, raw measurements. And the 10 feeders were the only team that got to see the actual animals. In particular, it seemed like the feeders functioned like quite the bottleneck. I'd love to get to observe all 1,000 animals, instead of just 10 messengers and transporters.

Anyways, that’s my job. Hope the giraffe is doing alright.

prompts.text:
Was reading "Lost in Backpropagation: The LM Head is a Gradient Bottleneck" by @nthngdy and @yoavartzi the other day. Their ideas seemed very clever, but my ability to follow their intuition was lacking. So I decided to imagine "What would it be like to work as a neuron", to better process their ideas. The main audience when writing this was just myself. Sharing in case others find it a fun read.

A Day in the Life of a Neuron Associate at Grub Zoo.
prompts.expected:
Welcome to Grub Zoo. Proud home of 1000 animals. Each animal has its own designated 5 minute feeding window during the day where it eats one serving of grub. The feeding schedule looks something like:
-Feed the horse and the Giraffe from 4:00-4:05.
-Feed the rhino from 4:15-4:20.
-Feed the 8 alligators from 7:10-7:15.

Initially the Zoo ran off a simple lookup chart, where one could query a 5 minute window, and get returned a list of all animals that needed to be fed. Well, Bob from Marketing had a great (terrible) idea to replace our lookup table with AI. But instead of using AI, we could just become AI (wtf?). He explained that we’d each get some role in a mega human neural network, then use the power of ‘backpropagation’ to tell each other what to do. I think this is his promo project or something, not sure. His idea is that the optimal feeding window should depend on all sorts of properties of the weather, and once we get this learning machine running, it can plug in a bunch of these advanced features.

The first part of the plan was to designate 10 employees as feeders. Each feeder had to write down how they would divvy up any grub they were given between the 1,000 animals. One feeder, Jeremy, decided he’d give all grub he was given to the sloth. Weird guy. Another one, Anna, decided she’d split up the grub equally across all 1,000 animals. (How’s she gonna manage that, lol?).

My job was the supplier. Every 5 minutes I’d show up with some servings of grub. Then I’d have to divvy it up between the feeders, who’d then divvy it up between the animals based on their prearranged fractions. The weird part here is that I was the only one who was aware of the time of day- the feeders always stuck to their fractions.

Bob said that during each 5 minute interval we’d have two phases: an execution phase, and a feedback phase. Well for the first 5 minute execution phase I frankly had no idea what was going on, so I just gave an equal amount of grub to each of the 10 feeders, who then distributed it out. Somehow Anna was able to get grub out to all 1,000 animals, impressive.

Only the horse and the giraffe were supposed to get fed in this window, but the small amount of grub ended up spread out across all animals, and nobody was happy. I voted to drop Bob’s idea, but he figured we could salvage things. His insight was “Most windows only have a couple animals who need getting fed, so after everybody distributes their grub, we should apply some sort of bunching action towards the ones with the most grub. That way at least somebody gets a decent meal. Sometimes multiple animals need grub and we won’t be sure we got it right, so just do soft bunching.” He called it softmax.

We applied his technique, and sure enough one animal got a good meal, but it was the wrong animal! And the animals at Grub Zoo are extremely picky about when they get fed! Well, Bob said this was ok at first (what?), we just needed the feedback phase.

The feedback phase started with the animals. The ones that didn’t get fed but were supposed to, complained loudly. The feeders were the only ones who could observe and hear the animals. Each feeder would first go observe all 1000 animals to see which ones were complaining. Then they’d update their fractions slightly towards giving them more grub. Now if the supplier had given the feeder little or no grub that window, the feeder would take little effort in updating their fraction as it wouldn’t matter anyway. But if they had been given a large amount of grub, they’d take tremendous honor in updating their fraction quite heavily. But they had to be careful here! They were going to use that fraction for every time window, so they didn’t want to over-correct for one 5 minute interval.

The next phase of feedback was for me as the supplier. Each of the 10 feeders came and told me either ‘Man I coulda made a difference I had the fractions right just give me more grub’, or ‘I was off on this one, didn’t need grub here’. Then my job was to update ‘Ok for this 5 minute interval, give grub to feeder X’, because they told me their fraction is calibrated. I figured none of the feeders had it exactly right, but if I gave more grub to the feeders that seemed decent at the right times, their errors would average out and softmax would help bunch it up on the right animals.

To me the process felt pretty dumb, as the feeders were just like mindless cogs, trying to find the one right fraction. They could see all 1000 animals. But all I could see were 10 people shouting ‘give me more/less grub’. And somehow I was supposed to manage all the windows from that?

Over time I developed a massive lookup table. For each 5 minute interval, how much grub to give to each of the 10 feeders. Each feeder started to get more sophisticated specialization. For instance, one guy fed just the 8 alligators. I knew to only give him grub from 7:10-7:15, because that’s when he complained.

Well, Bob got wind that I was using a lookup table for each 5 minute window and freaked out. Said it wasn’t true AI. Said I was getting demoted to a neuron. 9 other people got hired as neurons too, working in parallel to me.

Now instead of a unique fraction for each window, I had a simpler role. I had to learn a fixed ratio across the 10 feeders, and a simple rule for when to switch on. Initially I just put the fraction on for the morning. And then tuned the fraction a bit to give grub to the feeders that were clamoring for more grub in the morning. I figured if I helped focus on some of the morning intervals, other ‘neuron associates’ could manage other windows of the day. I never got to see what these other neuron associates were up to, but I figured if I listened to the feeders I could help compensate for the gaps.

Well, we got some new funding, and Bob decided to hire some more ‘neuron associates’, so we are up to 20 now. Communication is becoming a real problem. We never talk to each other, and it’s getting kind of weird only listening to the 10 feeders and trying to compensate for what all my coworkers are doing.

Now Bob had the craziest idea yet. He decided to break up our 20 neuron associates into two 10 member squads: Alpha and Bravo. I got put on Bravo. During each interval I’d get to see both the time of day, and how much the Alpha Squad was planning to give to each feeder. I decided to take on a targeted role: IF the time was between 10-11am AND I saw that Alpha Squad was giving grub to feeder 2, then I’d give grub to feeder 1 and 2. I learned that in the morning whenever Alpha Squad gave grub to feeder 2, feeder 2 would still complain and want even more, and feeder 1 complained as well.

I noticed that sometimes Alpha Squad would slip up and not give grub to feeder 2, which meant I didn’t trigger on feeder 1 or 2. When this happened, I’d complain loudly. Hey Alpha! Give more grub to feeder 2! Problem is, team Alpha was getting overwhelmed during the feedback cycle. They had to listen to both the feeders directly, and every single member on squad Bravo. The problem got even worse when we doubled the size of Alpha and Bravo to 20 people each. That’s when Bob started hiring a new role, called ‘transporters’ and ‘messengers’.

There was one messenger and transporter for each feeder. Everyone only got to receive feedback from the messengers, and give grub to the transporters. During the execution phase, the transporters would collect the grub from squad Alpha, then I could make my decision based on if transporter 2 had grub. All of us in squad Bravo would then add on to the grub the transporters were carrying. During the feedback phase, I’d tell messenger 2 if I wanted more grub sent to feeder 2. This way, Alpha squad didn’t have to talk to both the feeders and Bravo squad. The messengers just added up the feedback from both the feeders and Bravo.

We ran this operation for several weeks, with Alpha and Bravo squads distributing grub to the transporters, the messengers giving feedback, and the feeders divvying it out and observing the animals. It seemed like the dumbest thing I’d ever seen! A lookup table could have done the same thing!

Well, that’s when Bob made a change that actually blew my mind. He called it the ‘magic of generalization’. The first thing he did was give all neuron associates access to the temperature, in addition to the time of day. Now in the old world, we’d have to manually make updates to all 1000 animals in the lookup table to figure out how they responded to temperature. In the new world, I only had to change my allocation to the 10 transporters. The feeders had already built fractions that grouped the animals into correlated sets.

I developed a new trigger condition. IF the time was between 10-11am AND transporter 2 had grub AND the temperature was above 60F, then give grub to transporter 1, 2, and 3. I came to learn that in very cold weather, these messengers didn’t complain as much.

Over time Bob added new features I could trigger on. Rain. Wind. Sunshine. It was starting to be quite a lot to handle. Bob always had to go around explaining to every neuron associate how this new measurement would work. Eventually Bob got pretty tired of this. He decided that only squad Alpha could see things like time, temperature, rain, wind, and sunshine. At first this seemed completely crazy to me. How could I know when to trigger, without these key features?

We concocted a pretty funny plan. I noticed that messenger 9 NEVER complained. My guess is that feeder 9 was just completely checked-out. Never gave any grub to anyone. Team Alpha had picked up on this. They also knew that whenever it was between 10-11am and above 60F, messenger 2 would complain to them. So they decided to give grub to transporter 9 whenever it got hot in the morning- not because transporter 9 needed the grub. But because team Bravo could then use that signal to make better decisions.

I developed a new heuristic: IF transporter 2 AND transporter 9 have grub, then we give grub to transporter 1,2,3. AND we also take that grub away from transporter 9 and add it to the pile, since feeder 9 never complains.

So that became my job. I’d wake up every morning, drive in to work as a neuron associate, then pay very close attention to which 10 transporters had grub, and how that correlated to the complaints I’d get from the 10 messengers. I’d update my fractions among the 10 transporters, and update my feedback to the 10 messengers.

Later that month my team name got updated to Squad Bravo-46. What the heck? Turns out Bob had really scaled the operation. We now had 50 Bravo squads in series. My job was always the same, talk to 10 messengers, and observe 10 transporters. I had no idea what measurements got fed into Alpha Squad. And honestly, I had no idea how many animals even lived at the Zoo anymore. I didn’t even know how many team members were on Bravo-46, since I never talked to them.

Alpha Squad was the only team that got to see the pure, raw measurements. And the 10 feeders were the only team that got to see the actual animals. In particular, it seemed like the feeders functioned like quite the bottleneck. I'd love to get to observe all 1,000 animals, instead of just 10 messengers and transporters.

Anyways, that’s my job. Hope the giraffe is doing alright.

evalchemy209.title: Make Evalchemy results and resume state FineStore native
evalchemy209.body:
Write evaluation aggregates, normalized samples, and request checkpoints directly to FineStore. Resume restores committed requests by default. Before generation, the evaluator validates the stored task list and each task's fingerprint, including all supplied generation overrides. It initializes the model before this validation. Results and samples enter the archive in one transaction, so a retry leaves a completed result unchanged. FineStore result writes use the same guarded SymPy serialization as the CLI display.

`--output_path` and `--finestore_output_path` select the same FineStore archive. Existing scripts keep `--output_path` and use distinct archive paths for distinct evaluations. Native JSON/JSONL result serialization, SQLite resume state, temporary output staging, and the unused TACC listener are removed. The TACC distributed batch scripts remain. The serve-and-eval runner and regression gate read the same archive; the gate keeps `--results` as its archive selector. Concurrent writers to one archive have not been exercised locally.

Part of marin-community/marin#9972. The Marin retry work is tracked in marin-community/marin#9813.

msrl944.title: Refresh the frozen trainer stack to TE 2.20 and Torch 2.14.1
msrl944.body:
Refresh the combined trainer and serving group to Torch 2.14.1+cu132, CUDA 13.2.2, Transformer Engine 2.20.2, Core 0.19.2 and Bridge 0.6.2. Preserve Snowball and Hero MuonH/AdamH math, BF16 compute, FP32 state and router biases, HF import/export, expert routes, repeated weight transfer and fresh-stack save/resume. The recipe and qualified baseline evidence are in https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/610.

Use native FlashAttention versioning, event loops, Core attention selection and expert tags, NCCL transport selection and batch-invariance initialization, and W&B mutable tables. Remove obsolete vLLM API branches, global broadcast replacement, unconditional compile/sampler overrides, wheel migration tools, dead FP8/Qwen helpers, the extra Ray peer-access allocation, copied NCCL settings and startup staggering. Native Harbor already includes its config module, so remove the overlapping standalone distribution. The default uv prerelease policy preserves all 510 package records. Retained fixes have source links and removal conditions beside the code; existing packaging checks refuse unverified runtime, patch-source and build inputs.

The serving changes are in [vLLM PR95](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/95). This draft still selects the qualified [3a wheel pair](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20261012-3a054c458ca8) until the source receives the required GitHub review, lands normally and the official main-only build publishes qualified artifacts. Its native FFI 0.1.11, TileLang 0.1.12 and Tokenspeed MLA 0.1.8 group must then be adopted coherently with [Marin PR10022](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10022). The new published Marin package/projection path and other affected application paths still require qualification.

Focused removal pilots passed 17 cases on H100 and 16 on GB200; a cold GB200 FlashInfer build exceeded the startup deadline and completed separately in 2,464 seconds. A two-GB200 native initializer/shared-group probe passed 18 exact broadcasts without copied NCCL settings. Tiny native Core/MSC S3 save/load passes, while five alternating reader comparisons support retaining record buffering: 69 native GETs versus 9 maintained GETs per read, with exact values in both. Removing Hero's CUDA graph guard produced NaN logprobs after changing batch sizes; retain it. These component results do not qualify the final packaged runtime, full-model continuation or RL throughput.

The bounded High source review and targeted follow-ups found no remaining source blocker. The original four full-model reports apply to the baseline; reuse requires explicit source, lock, payload, build-input and exercised-path comparison. The remaining compiler, dependency-metadata, checkpoint and reload fixes remain maintenance costs. Optional HDO, SGLang, GPTOSS, sandbox and legacy fidelity/cache paths are separate from the required MuonH profile and are not qualified by these pilots.

Keep the qualified fallback branch and artifacts. Final consumer merges remain Romain's actions after final artifacts, affected Snowball/Hero and performance gates, coherent pins and terminal CI. The [native Snowball checkpoint oracle failure](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9400#issuecomment-6129427326), parked [TPU pair](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10023), original Hero/GB200 shutdown anomaly and optimizer-payload sampling limits remain disclosed. Policy-only TE timings do not establish full RL throughput or performance equivalence.

evalchemy214.title: Separate grading from score aggregation
evalchemy214.body:
Use each benchmark's aggregation code for both normal evaluation and partial-result recovery, preserving its metrics and breakdowns. Save grading evidence before aggregation so it can be replayed without rerunning graders.

Repeated evaluations with infrastructure-failed trials still fail the task.
